name: Giotto di Bondone
bio: Often called the first great painter of the Renaissance, Giotto gave figures real bulk, weight and human feeling. His fresco cycle in Padua's Scrovegni Chapel set the course of Western narrative painting.
bio_full: Giotto di Bondone was born around 1267 in the Mugello valley near Florence, probably at Colle di Vespignano. According to a famous legend told by Vasari, the painter Cimabue discovered him as a shepherd boy drawing his sheep on a rock and took him on as a pupil. Giotto worked across Italy: in Rome, in Assisi, where the fresco cycle of the life of St Francis in the Upper Church is traditionally but debatably attributed to him, in Padua, Naples and Milan. His greatest surviving work is the fresco cycle of the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua (around 1305). Late in life he was appointed chief architect of Florence Cathedral and designed its bell tower, still known as Giotto's Campanile. He died in Florence in 1337.

Giotto broke with the flat, stylised conventions of Byzantine painting. He gave his figures real weight and volume, placed them in believable spaces, and showed human emotion with a new directness and dignity, so that sacred stories became human dramas. Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio praised him in his own time, and Renaissance writers saw him as the artist who began the revival of painting. He is often called the father of Western painting.

name: Donatello
bio: The most inventive sculptor of the early Renaissance, Donatello revived the classical nude and free-standing bronze statue. He worked in marble, bronze, wood and terracotta with striking psychological realism.
bio_full: Donato di Niccolò di Betto Bardi, known as Donatello, trained in Ghiberti's bronze workshop before becoming the most inventive sculptor of the 15th century. His early marble saints for Orsanmichele and Florence Cathedral, such as St Mark and St George, gave figures a new psychological life and a believable stance. He also invented rilievo schiacciato ('flattened relief'), creating deep perspective in carving only millimetres deep. His friend and patron was Cosimo de' Medici.

Donatello revived antique types that had not been made for a thousand years, including the free-standing nude and the bronze equestrian monument (the Gattamelata in Padua, 1453). His late works, such as the gaunt wooden Penitent Magdalene, have a raw intensity that looks ahead to much later art. He was buried near Cosimo in the church of San Lorenzo.

name: Sandro Botticelli
bio: A Florentine painter close to the Medici circle, known for graceful line and mythological subjects drawn from Neoplatonic philosophy. His work fell out of favour for centuries before being rediscovered in the 19th century.
bio_full: Alessandro Filipepi, known as Sandro Botticelli, trained with Fra Filippo Lippi and became one of the favourite painters of the Medici circle under Lorenzo the Magnificent. In 1481–82 he was one of the artists summoned to Rome to fresco the walls of the new Sistine Chapel. He produced altarpieces, portraits, tondos (round paintings) and a long series of drawings illustrating Dante's Divine Comedy.

Botticelli's art is built on flowing line, graceful elongated figures and a melancholy beauty. His mythological paintings reflect the Neoplatonic philosophy of Lorenzo's circle, in which pagan myth could express Christian and moral truths. In the 1490s the friar Savonarola preached against luxury and pagan art in Florence. Botticelli's later work grows more severe and religious, and he died largely forgotten. The Pre-Raphaelites and Aesthetic movement of the 19th century revived him, and he is now among the most popular painters in the world.

portrait_caption: Presumed self-portrait, detail of the Adoration of the Magi, c. 1475

name: Jan van Eyck
bio: Court painter to the Duke of Burgundy, van Eyck brought oil painting to an unmatched level of luminous detail. His portraits and altarpieces fuse close observation with layered religious symbolism.
bio_full: Jan van Eyck is first recorded working for John of Bavaria in The Hague. From 1425 he was court painter and valet de chambre to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, one of the richest rulers in Europe. Philip valued him highly enough to send him on confidential diplomatic missions, including a voyage to Portugal in 1428–29 to paint the portrait of the duke's prospective bride, Isabella. He settled in Bruges, where he died in 1441. He sometimes signed with the punning motto 'Als ich can' ('As I can').

Van Eyck did not invent oil paint, as later legend claimed, but he perfected it. By building up thin, translucent glazes he achieved glowing colour and an unprecedented level of detail: individual hairs, reflections in metal and pearls, the texture of fur and brocade. His portraits are among the first independent portraits in Western art, and his religious works pack everyday objects with symbolic meaning. Italian collectors prized his work, and he shaped the whole tradition of Netherlandish painting.

portrait_caption: Portrait of a Man (Man in a Red Turban), 1433, possibly a self-portrait

name: Hieronymus Bosch
bio: Bosch painted teeming moral allegories full of hybrid creatures, temptations and punishments. His imagination later made him a hero to the Surrealists.
bio_full: Jheronimus van Aken took the name Bosch from his home town of 's-Hertogenbosch in the Duchy of Brabant, where his family were painters and where he spent almost his whole life. Few documents about him survive. We know that he married into a wealthy family and was a prominent member of the religious Brotherhood of Our Lady, and that his patrons included the Burgundian and Habsburg nobility. Only around 25 paintings are firmly attributed to him today.

Bosch painted moral and religious allegories crowded with tiny figures, hybrid monsters, strange architecture and burning landscapes, warning of sin, folly and damnation. His meaning has been debated for centuries, with readings ranging from orthodox sermon to secret heresy. Philip II of Spain was an avid collector, which is why the Prado holds many of his greatest works. His teeming imagination influenced Bruegel and, centuries later, was claimed by the Surrealists.

name: Albrecht Dürer
bio: Painter, printmaker and theorist who carried Italian Renaissance ideas north of the Alps. His woodcuts and engravings circulated across Europe and made him the first internationally famous artist through print.
bio_full: Albrecht Dürer was the son of a Hungarian-born goldsmith in Nuremberg, a wealthy imperial city and printing centre. He trained as a goldsmith and then with the painter Michael Wolgemut, travelled as a journeyman, and made two journeys to Italy (1494–95 and 1505–07), where he absorbed Venetian colour and Italian theory. His woodcut series the Apocalypse (1498) made him famous across Europe. He later worked for Emperor Maximilian I and travelled to the Netherlands in 1520–21, leaving a vivid diary of the journey.

Dürer was painter, draughtsman, engraver, theorist and a shrewd businessman. He published his own prints and protected his famous 'AD' monogram, and late in life he wrote treatises on measurement, fortification and human proportion. He made self-portraiting a serious art and raised printmaking to the level of painting. He was the first northern artist to absorb the Italian Renaissance fully, and he became the model of the artist as intellectual.

name: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
bio: Bruegel painted peasant life, proverbs and landscapes with humour and humanity. His seasonal landscapes are among the first great pure landscape paintings in Europe.
bio_full: Pieter Bruegel the Elder probably came from the region of Breda. He became a master in the Antwerp painters' guild in 1551 and soon travelled to Italy, crossing the Alps, whose mountain scenery later filled his landscapes. Back in Antwerp he designed prints for the publisher Hieronymus Cock, including Bosch-like moral allegories. In 1563 he married Mayken Coecke, the daughter of his former master, and moved to Brussels. He died there in 1569. His sons Pieter Brueghel the Younger and Jan Brueghel the Elder founded a long dynasty of painters.

Bruegel painted peasant weddings and dances, children's games, proverbs, biblical scenes set in contemporary Flanders and the cycle of the seasons, with humour, sharp observation and deep humanity. Later legend made him 'Peasant Bruegel', but he was a learned city-dweller who moved in humanist circles and sold to wealthy collectors. His panoramic landscapes and his view of human folly within the vastness of nature are among the most original achievements of 16th-century art.

portrait_caption: The Painter and the Buyer, drawing, c. 1566, often taken as a self-portrait

name: Leonardo da Vinci
bio: The archetypal Renaissance polymath: painter, engineer, anatomist and inventor. Fewer than twenty paintings survive, but his soft modelling (sfumato) and psychological depth transformed painting.
bio_full: Leonardo was the illegitimate son of a Florentine notary, born in the hill town of Vinci. He trained in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, where, according to Vasari, the angel he painted in Verrocchio's Baptism of Christ outshone his master's work. In 1482 he moved to Milan in the service of Duke Ludovico Sforza, working as painter, engineer, pageant designer and sculptor of a colossal equestrian monument that was never cast. After the French invaded Milan in 1499 he moved between Florence, Milan and Rome. He spent his last years in France as the guest of King Francis I and died at Amboise in 1519.

Leonardo finished few paintings, but each changed the art. He invented sfumato, the soft smoky blending of light and shade, and gave his figures inner psychological life. His notebooks, of which around 7,000 pages survive, are written in mirror script. They record studies in anatomy, optics, geology, botany, flight, hydraulics and war machines, based on careful observation centuries ahead of their time. He has become the archetype of the 'Renaissance man'.

portrait_caption: Portrait drawing by Francesco Melzi, c. 1515–18

name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
bio: Sculptor first, but also painter, architect and poet. His heroic, muscular figures dominate the High Renaissance, and his late work points toward Mannerism.
bio_full: Michelangelo Buonarroti was born in Caprese and raised in Florence. He was briefly apprenticed to the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio and then studied sculpture in the circle of Lorenzo de' Medici. Before he was 30 he had carved the Rome Pietà and the David. Pope Julius II then called him to Rome for a vast tomb project that dragged on for 40 years, and made him paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling. He went on to design the Medici Chapel and Laurentian Library in Florence and, from 1546, served as chief architect of St Peter's Basilica, designing its great dome. He died in Rome in 1564, aged 88.

Michelangelo saw himself above all as a sculptor who released figures from the stone. His art is centred on the heroic male nude, charged with muscular energy and spiritual struggle, and he also wrote passionate poetry, including sonnets to Vittoria Colonna and Tommaso de' Cavalieri. Contemporaries called him 'il divino'. Vasari's Lives presented him as the summit of all art, and his towering reputation shaped the modern idea of artistic genius.
portrait_file: Michelangelo Daniele da Volterra (dettaglio).jpg
portrait_caption: Portrait by Daniele da Volterra, c. 1544

name: Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio)
bio: Raphael synthesised the lessons of Leonardo and Michelangelo into a style of perfect clarity and grace. He ran a large workshop in Rome for the papacy before dying at 37.
bio_full: Raffaello Sanzio was the son of Giovanni Santi, a painter and poet at the cultivated court of Urbino. He was orphaned young and absorbed the graceful style of Pietro Perugino before moving to Florence around 1504, where he studied Leonardo and Michelangelo. In 1508 Julius II brought him to Rome to decorate the papal apartments (the Stanze). Under Leo X he became the most important artist in the city: painter, designer of tapestries for the Sistine Chapel, architect of St Peter's after Bramante, and superintendent of Roman antiquities. He died on his 37th birthday in 1520 and was buried in the Pantheon.

Raphael's art combines clarity, harmony and grace. His Madonnas became the most beloved religious images in Europe, and his large frescoes organise dozens of figures with effortless balance. He ran an efficient workshop and worked closely with printmakers, so his designs spread widely. For three centuries academies held him up as the model of perfect painting, which is why the 19th-century Pre-Raphaelites defined themselves against him.

name: Titian (Tiziano Vecellio)
birthplace: Pieve di Cadore, Republic of Venice
bio: Leader of the Venetian school, Titian built paintings from colour rather than line. His loose late brushwork anticipated painters from Rubens to the Impressionists.
bio_full: Tiziano Vecellio came to Venice from the Alpine town of Pieve di Cadore as a boy. He trained with Giovanni Bellini, worked with Giorgione and, after Bellini's death in 1516, became the city's leading painter. His fame spread across Europe. He painted for the dukes of Ferrara, Mantua and Urbino, and above all for the Emperor Charles V, who made him a Count Palatine and a knight, and for Philip II of Spain. For Philip he painted a series of mythologies he called 'poesie'. He died in Venice in 1576 during a plague epidemic, in his late eighties.

Titian built his paintings from colour rather than drawing, and he excelled in every genre: altarpieces, mythologies, nudes and portraits that set the pattern for state portraiture. In old age his brushwork became extraordinarily loose. He reportedly painted with his fingers and returned to canvases again and again, creating flickering surfaces that seemed almost unfinished. Rubens, Velázquez, Rembrandt, Delacroix and the Impressionists all learned from him.
portrait_file: Titian - Self-portrait (Museo del Prado).jpg

name: El Greco (Domenikos Theotokopoulos)
bio: Trained as an icon painter in Crete, then in Venice and Rome, El Greco settled in Toledo. His elongated, flickering figures and visionary colour were rediscovered by early modernists.
bio_full: Domenikos Theotokopoulos was born in Candia on Crete, then ruled by Venice, and was already a master painter of icons there. Around 1567 he moved to Venice, where he absorbed Titian and Tintoretto, and then to Rome. In 1577 he went to Spain, hoping for the patronage of Philip II at the Escorial, but the king disliked his work. He settled in Toledo, where he lived until his death in 1614, painting altarpieces, saints and portraits for the city's churches and intellectual elite. He always signed his works in Greek.

El Greco fused Byzantine spirituality, Venetian colour and Mannerist elongation into one of the most personal styles in art. His figures are flame-like and stretched, set in flickering light and unearthly colours. After his death he was largely dismissed as eccentric. He was rediscovered in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when artists such as Cézanne, Picasso and the German Expressionists saw him as a forerunner of modern art.

portrait_caption: Portrait of a Man, c. 1595–1600, probably a self-portrait

name: Caravaggio (Michelangelo Merisi)
bio: Caravaggio used street models and dramatic spotlighting (tenebrism) to make sacred scenes startlingly real. His violent life was as famous as his art, and his followers spread his style across Europe.
bio_full: Michelangelo Merisi was born in Milan in 1571 into a family from the nearby town of Caravaggio, which gave him his name. He trained with the Milanese painter Simone Peterzano and arrived in Rome in the early 1590s, poor and unknown. He first made his name with still lifes and half-length paintings of young men, then found a powerful patron in Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte. His public breakthrough came in 1600 with the Saint Matthew paintings for the Contarelli Chapel. Records show repeated arrests for brawling, carrying weapons and assault. In 1606 he killed Ranuccio Tomassoni in a fight and fled Rome under a death sentence. He worked in Naples, Malta (where he was briefly made a Knight of St John before being imprisoned and expelled), and Sicily. He died in 1610 at Porto Ercole, on his way back to Rome to seek a papal pardon.

Caravaggio painted saints and biblical figures from ordinary street models, with dirty feet, wrinkled faces and torn clothes, and plunged them into deep shadow cut by a raking spotlight. This dramatic technique is known as tenebrism. His radical realism shocked some patrons, and several altarpieces were rejected. It also inspired a generation of followers across Europe, the Caravaggisti, from Utrecht to Naples and Seville, and transformed Baroque painting.
portrait_file: Bild-Ottavio Leoni, Caravaggio.jpg
portrait_caption: Portrait drawing by Ottavio Leoni, c. 1621

name: Artemisia Gentileschi
bio: One of the most accomplished followers of Caravaggio and the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. She specialised in powerful heroines from the Bible and history.
bio_full: Artemisia Gentileschi was the daughter of the painter Orazio Gentileschi, a follower of Caravaggio, and trained in his Roman studio. In 1611, at about 17, she was raped by the painter Agostino Tassi, her father's collaborator. At the trial that followed in 1612 she was tortured with thumbscrews to test her testimony. Tassi was convicted but barely punished. Soon after, she married and moved to Florence. There she won the patronage of the Medici and in 1616 became the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. She later worked in Rome, Venice, Naples and London, where she joined her father at the court of Charles I around 1638–40, before settling in Naples.

Artemisia specialised in strong women from the Bible and history: Judith, Susanna, Esther, Cleopatra, Lucretia and Mary Magdalene. She painted them with powerful realism, dramatic light and psychological depth. She was celebrated in her lifetime and then largely forgotten. Feminist art historians rediscovered her from the 1970s on, and major exhibitions, including one at the National Gallery in London in 2020, have established her as one of the great painters of the Baroque.
portrait_file: Self-portrait as the Allegory of Painting (La Pittura) - Artemisia Gentileschi.jpg
portrait_caption: Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting, c. 1638–39

name: Peter Paul Rubens
bio: Painter, diplomat and scholar who ran a huge Antwerp studio. His energetic compositions and fleshy figures define the Flemish Baroque.
bio_full: Peter Paul Rubens was born in Siegen in Germany, where his Protestant father had fled, and grew up in Antwerp after the family returned and converted to Catholicism. After his training he spent 1600–08 in Italy, mainly at the Gonzaga court in Mantua, studying Michelangelo, Titian and ancient sculpture. Back in Antwerp he became court painter to the Habsburg governors Archduke Albert and Isabella and built a grand house and studio, now the Rubenshuis museum. He ran a huge workshop, with assistants such as the young Anthony van Dyck, and produced altarpieces, mythologies, portraits, tapestry designs and vast decorative cycles, including the life of Marie de' Medici (Louvre) and the ceiling of the Banqueting House in Whitehall.

Rubens was also a highly educated humanist and a diplomat. He helped negotiate peace between Spain and England in 1629–30 and was knighted by both Charles I and Philip IV. His paintings are full of energy, swirling movement, warm colour and abundant flesh, which gave English the word 'Rubenesque'. He was the most influential painter of the northern Baroque, and later painters from Watteau to Delacroix and Renoir looked to him.
portrait_file: Peter Paul Rubens - Self-portrait - RH.S.180 - Rubenshuis (after restoration).jpg

name: Gian Lorenzo Bernini
bio: The supreme sculptor and architect of Baroque Rome, he made marble appear to move, breathe and soften. He also designed the colonnade of St Peter's Square.
bio_full: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was born in Naples, the son of the sculptor Pietro Bernini, and moved to Rome as a child. By his early twenties he had carved a series of dazzling marble groups for Cardinal Scipione Borghese: Pluto and Proserpina, Apollo and Daphne and a David. His great patron Pope Urban VIII put him in charge of St Peter's, where he created the bronze baldacchino over the high altar, the Cathedra Petri, and the vast colonnaded piazza. He also designed the Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona, the church of Sant'Andrea al Quirinale and many papal tombs and busts. In 1665 Louis XIV invited him to Paris to design the Louvre, but his plans were not adopted.

Bernini made marble appear to breathe, soften and move: flesh dimples under fingers, hair streams in the wind, and stone becomes leaves. He fused sculpture, architecture, painting and hidden light into total theatrical experiences, and he also wrote and staged plays. More than any other artist he defined the look of Baroque Rome, and his long rivalry with the architect Francesco Borromini is one of the great stories of art history.
portrait_file: Gian Lorenzo Bernini, self-portrait, c1623.jpg

name: Diego Velázquez
bio: Court painter to Philip IV of Spain, admired for his virtuoso, economical brushwork and penetrating portraits. Manet called him 'the painter of painters'.
bio_full: Diego Velázquez was born in Seville and trained with the painter and theorist Francisco Pacheco, whose daughter Juana he married. His early works include bodegones, kitchen scenes with figures painted with sober realism. In 1623 he became painter to the young King Philip IV in Madrid, where he spent the rest of his career. He took on increasingly important court offices, including palace chamberlain, organising royal events. He travelled to Italy twice, in 1629–31 and 1649–51, studying Titian and the antique and buying art for the royal collection. In 1659 he was admitted to the noble Order of Santiago, and he died in Madrid the following year.

Velázquez's art moved from early tight realism to an astonishingly free, economical brushwork. Seen up close his paintings dissolve into loose dabs of paint, but from a distance they resolve into silk, lace, flesh and air. He painted kings, the court's jesters and dwarfs, mythologies and the only surviving Spanish female nude of the period, the Rokeby Venus. Manet called him 'the painter of painters'. Goya, the Impressionists, Picasso and Francis Bacon all studied him.
portrait_file: Diego Velázquez Autorretrato 45 x 38 cm - Colección Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Carlos - Museo de Bellas Artes de Valencia.jpg
portrait_caption: Self-portrait, c. 1640s, Museo de Bellas Artes, Valencia

name: Rembrandt van Rijn
bio: The greatest painter of the Dutch Golden Age, celebrated for dramatic light, deep humanity and a lifelong series of self-portraits. He was also a master etcher.
bio_full: Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was the son of a Leiden miller. He trained there and briefly in Amsterdam with the history painter Pieter Lastman, then moved permanently to Amsterdam in the early 1630s. The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp (1632) made his name. He married Saskia van Uylenburgh, bought a grand house and collected art and curiosities extravagantly. Saskia died in 1642, the year of The Night Watch, and of their children only their son Titus survived infancy. Lavish spending and the economic climate led to his insolvency in 1656, and he lost his house and collection. His later years were marked by the deaths of his partner Hendrickje Stoffels and of Titus. He died in Amsterdam in 1669.

Rembrandt was a supreme painter, draughtsman and etcher. His art is famed for dramatic chiaroscuro, rich, sometimes thickly built-up paint and a deep empathy for human emotion, whether in biblical scenes, portraits of Amsterdam burghers or the more than 80 self-portraits in paint, etching and drawing that trace his face from youth to old age. Scholars have long debated attributions, and the Rembrandt Research Project spent decades sorting his works from those of his many pupils.
portrait_file: Rembrandt Self-portrait (Kenwood).jpg

name: Johannes Vermeer
bio: Vermeer painted quiet domestic interiors bathed in pearly daylight. Only about 35 works are attributed to him, and he was largely forgotten until the 19th century.
bio_full: Johannes Vermeer spent his whole life in Delft, where his father was a weaver, innkeeper and art dealer. He joined the painters' Guild of St Luke in 1653 and later served as its head. He married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic, and they lived in the house of her well-off mother, Maria Thins. They had 15 children, 11 of whom survived him. He seems to have worked slowly, producing perhaps two or three paintings a year, and around 35 survive. In 1672 the French invasion of the Dutch Republic wrecked the art market, and he died in 1675 leaving his family in debt.

Vermeer painted quiet interiors, mostly of women reading letters, playing music, pouring milk or making lace, by a window that floods the room with soft daylight. He used expensive natural ultramarine, sparkling dots of light (pointillé) and precise perspective, and some scholars believe he used optical devices such as the camera obscura. He was almost forgotten until the French critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger championed him in the 1860s. Today he is one of the most admired painters in the world.
portrait_file: Cropped version of Jan Vermeer van Delft 002.jpg
portrait_caption: Figure in The Procuress, 1656, often thought to be a self-portrait

name: Antoine Watteau
bio: Inventor of the fête galante, a scene of elegant figures flirting in dreamy parkland. His wistful mood set the tone for the Rococo.
bio_full: Antoine Watteau was born in Valenciennes, a town recently annexed to France, and arrived in Paris around 1702. He worked for the theatre painter Claude Gillot, who gave him a lifelong love of the commedia dell'arte. He then worked for the decorator Claude Audran, through whom he could study Rubens's Medici cycle in the Luxembourg Palace. He was admitted to the Royal Academy in 1712, although it took him five years to deliver his reception piece. He suffered from tuberculosis, visited London in 1719–20 to consult a doctor, and died in 1721 aged only 36.

Watteau invented a new genre, the fête galante: elegant men and women in silks lingering in dreamy parks, flirting, making music and dressed as theatre characters. His feathery brushwork, shimmering colour and the faint melancholy beneath the pleasure gave the Rococo its tone. His last great work, the shop sign for the art dealer Gersaint (Berlin), shows paintings being sold and packed. Its scene of Louis XIV's portrait being crated has been read as the end of an era.
portrait_file: (Treviso) The painter Antoine Watteau by Rosalba Carriera - Museo civico di Santa Caterina.jpg

name: Jean-Honoré Fragonard
bio: A brilliant, rapid painter of love scenes and gardens for aristocratic patrons. The French Revolution ended demand for his work.
bio_full: Jean-Honoré Fragonard was born in Grasse in Provence and grew up in Paris. He briefly studied with Chardin and then with Boucher. He won the Prix de Rome in 1752 and spent several years in Italy, sketching the gardens of Roman villas. In 1765 the Academy acclaimed his grand history painting Coresus and Callirhoë, but he then largely abandoned official careers to work for wealthy private clients. His series The Progress of Love, made for Madame du Barry, was returned to him and is now in the Frick Collection, New York.

Fragonard painted playful scenes of love, gardens, children and reading with dazzling, rapid brushwork, as well as his virtuoso 'fantasy figures', each painted in about an hour. The French Revolution destroyed his aristocratic market. Jacques-Louis David helped him find a post in the administration of the new Louvre museum, but he died in 1806 almost forgotten, and he was rediscovered by 19th-century collectors and painters.
portrait_file: Jean-Honoré Fragonard - Self-portrait with smiling face.jpg

name: Jacques-Louis David
bio: The leading Neoclassical painter, an active revolutionary and later Napoleon's official painter. He died in exile in Brussels after the Bourbon restoration.
bio_full: Jacques-Louis David was born in Paris in 1748. He trained with Joseph-Marie Vien and, after several failed attempts, won the Prix de Rome in 1774. In Rome (1775–80) he immersed himself in ancient sculpture and Poussin, and his Oath of the Horatii caused a sensation at the Paris Salon of 1785. During the Revolution he became a radical Jacobin deputy to the National Convention, voted for the execution of Louis XVI and staged great public festivals. After Robespierre's fall in 1794 he was imprisoned for a time. He then became the official painter of Napoleon, recording his coronation in a vast canvas (1805–07). After the restoration of the Bourbons he was exiled as a regicide to Brussels, where he died in 1825.

David was the leader of Neoclassicism. His paintings use clear, sculptural drawing, severe compositions, restrained colour and subjects of civic virtue and self-sacrifice drawn from Greek and Roman history. He also painted penetrating portraits. His studio trained a whole generation, including Gros, Girodet, Gérard and Ingres, and his work shows how art could serve politics and propaganda.
portrait_file: David Self Portrait.jpg

name: Antonio Canova
bio: The most celebrated Neoclassical sculptor, famous for marble of extraordinary smoothness and grace. He also helped recover art looted by Napoleon.
bio_full: Antonio Canova was the grandson of a stonemason in Possagno, in the Venetian foothills. He trained in Venice and moved to Rome in 1781, where his tomb of Pope Clement XIV quickly made him famous. He became the most celebrated sculptor in Europe and worked for popes, the Napoleonic family, Russian tsars and British collectors. His works include Pauline Bonaparte Borghese as Venus Victrix, a colossal nude Napoleon as Mars the Peacemaker (now in Apsley House, London) and the Three Graces. In 1815 the Pope sent him to Paris to negotiate the return of artworks looted by Napoleon, and he was rewarded with a noble title.

Canova's marble is famous for its almost luminous smoothness, achieved with special polishing and a final wax patina, and for its ideal, graceful figures and delicate balance of sensuality and calm. He is the defining sculptor of Neoclassicism. He designed and paid for a temple in his home town, where he is buried, and his studio models are kept in a museum there.
portrait_file: Antonio Canova Selfportrait 1792.jpg

name: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
bio: A pupil of David and champion of line over colour, Ingres was the great rival of Delacroix. His portraits and odalisques combine cool precision with sensual distortion.
bio_full: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was born in Montauban, the son of a decorative artist, and showed early talent for both drawing and the violin. He trained in David's studio in Paris and won the Prix de Rome in 1801. He spent the years 1806–24 in Rome and Florence, often supporting himself by making exquisite portrait drawings of tourists. His Vow of Louis XIII at the Salon of 1824 made him the champion of the classical tradition against Delacroix's Romanticism. He later directed the French Academy in Rome and continued to paint into his eighties, finishing The Turkish Bath in 1862.

Ingres declared that 'drawing is the probity of art'. His paintings are defined by pure, flowing contour, smooth surfaces and an ideal beauty derived from Raphael and Greek vases, yet he often bent anatomy for the sake of graceful line. His portraits, such as Monsieur Bertin and Madame Moitessier, are among the most compelling of the 19th century. His mix of classicism and sensual distortion influenced Degas, Matisse and Picasso. In French, 'violon d'Ingres' means a hobby, after his love of the violin.

name: Francisco Goya
bio: Court painter to the Spanish crown who became an unsparing witness to war, cruelty and superstition. His late 'Black Paintings' and print series point straight toward modern art.
bio_full: Francisco de Goya was born in Fuendetodos near Zaragoza and trained in Zaragoza and Madrid, with a visit to Italy. He made his name designing cartoons for the Royal Tapestry Factory, cheerful scenes of Spanish life, and rose to become First Court Painter to Charles IV in 1799. A severe illness in 1792–93 left him completely deaf, and his art grew darker and more personal. His print series Los Caprichos (1799) satirised superstition and corruption. The French invasion and the brutal Peninsular War (1808–14) produced his etchings The Disasters of War, published only after his death. In 1819–23 he painted the 'Black Paintings' on the walls of his house outside Madrid, and in 1824 he went into self-imposed exile in Bordeaux, where he died in 1828.

Goya was a brilliant court portraitist and painter of the Spanish people. He was also an unsparing witness to war, cruelty, madness and the irrational, and he anticipated Romanticism, Expressionism and even Surrealism. His Family of Charles IV, his Majas and his prints made him a crucial link between Velázquez and modern artists such as Manet and Picasso.

name: Caspar David Friedrich
bio: The key German Romantic painter, known for solitary figures facing vast, spiritual landscapes. His work fell into obscurity until the early 20th century.
bio_full: Caspar David Friedrich was born in Greifswald on the Baltic coast, then part of Swedish Pomerania. His childhood was marked by loss: his mother died when he was seven, and a brother drowned trying to save him when he fell through the ice. He studied at the Copenhagen Academy and from 1798 settled in Dresden. A prize from Goethe in 1805 and his controversial Tetschen Altarpiece (The Cross in the Mountains, 1808), a landscape used as an altarpiece, brought him attention. In 1810 the Prussian crown prince bought The Monk by the Sea and The Abbey in the Oakwood. After a stroke in 1835 he could barely paint, and he died in poverty and obscurity in 1840.

Friedrich turned landscape into a vehicle for religious and philosophical meaning: moonrises, Gothic ruins, misty mountains, Baltic shores and frozen seas, often with solitary figures seen from behind (Rückenfiguren) gazing into the infinite. His paintings embody the Romantic sublime and the individual's relationship with nature and God. Forgotten after his death, he was rediscovered in an exhibition in Berlin in 1906, and his influence can be traced to Munch and the Abstract Expressionists.

name: J. M. W. Turner
bio: Turner dissolved landscape into light, storm and atmosphere. His late canvases were so free that they seemed nearly abstract to contemporaries.
bio_full: Joseph Mallord William Turner was born in Covent Garden, London, the son of a barber. He entered the Royal Academy Schools at 14, exhibited there at 15, and was elected a full Academician in 1802, aged only 26. He travelled tirelessly through Britain and Europe, the Alps, the Rhine and above all Venice, filling hundreds of sketchbooks, and was also a master of watercolour and an important printmaker. Eccentric and secretive, he lived his last years in Chelsea under the name 'Mr Booth'. He died in 1851 and left the nation his studio contents: around 300 oil paintings and some 30,000 works on paper, now mostly at Tate Britain.

Turner began in the tradition of Claude Lorrain and the Dutch marine painters, but he increasingly dissolved landscape into light, colour, storm, fire, steam and atmosphere. His late works were mocked as incomprehensible by some critics and championed by the young John Ruskin. Turner is seen as a forerunner of Impressionism and even abstraction. Britain's leading contemporary art prize is named after him, and his self-portrait and The Fighting Temeraire appear on the £20 note.

name: John Constable
bio: Constable painted the English countryside from direct observation, with fresh skies and flecks of light. He was more admired in France than in Britain during his lifetime.
bio_full: John Constable was born in East Bergholt, Suffolk, the son of a prosperous mill-owner and corn merchant whose mills at Flatford and Dedham stood on the River Stour. He entered the Royal Academy Schools in 1799 but found recognition slowly. His long courtship of Maria Bicknell was opposed by her family until they married in 1816. He spent summers in Hampstead, where he made famous cloud studies in 1821–22, which he called 'skying'. His work won a gold medal in Paris in 1824, but he was elected a full Royal Academician only in 1829, aged 52, the year after Maria's death.

Constable painted the familiar landscape of the Stour valley ('Constable Country'), Salisbury, Hampstead and Brighton with fresh observation, broken touches of colour, and flecks of white to capture glittering light, which critics called 'Constable's snow'. He made full-size oil sketches for his large 'six-footer' exhibition canvases. He was more admired in France than in England during his lifetime, and he influenced Delacroix, the Barbizon School and the Impressionists.

name: Théodore Géricault
bio: A pioneer of French Romanticism who turned a contemporary scandal into monumental history painting. He died at 32 after a riding accident.
bio_full: Théodore Géricault was born in Rouen to a wealthy family and became a passionate horseman. He trained with Carle Vernet and Pierre-Narcisse Guérin and made a sensational debut at the 1812 Salon with The Charging Chasseur. After studying in Italy in 1816–17 he devoted 18 months to The Raft of the Medusa, exhibited in 1819. He visited England in 1820–21, painting horse races and the London poor. Around 1822 he painted a series of portraits of the mentally ill for a psychiatrist friend. Riding accidents and illness led to his death in 1824, aged just 32.

In his short career Géricault rejected the cool idealism of David's school for raw energy, dramatic contrast and contemporary subjects charged with suffering and political meaning. His studies of horses, corpses and severed limbs and his portraits of 'monomaniacs' show a new psychological and physical realism. He opened the way for French Romanticism and for Delacroix, who admired him deeply.

name: Eugène Delacroix
bio: Leader of French Romantic painting, devoted to colour, movement and exotic or literary subjects. His handling of colour deeply influenced the Impressionists.
bio_full: Eugène Delacroix was born at Charenton-Saint-Maurice near Paris. Rumours have long suggested that the statesman Talleyrand was his real father. He trained with Pierre-Narcisse Guérin, studied Rubens and Venetian painters in the Louvre, and was profoundly influenced by Géricault. The Barque of Dante (1822), The Massacre at Chios (1824) and The Death of Sardanapalus (1827) made him the leader of the Romantic school. A journey to Morocco and Algeria in 1832 gave him a lifelong store of exotic subjects. He also painted vast decorative schemes in the Palais Bourbon, the Louvre and the church of Saint-Sulpice, and kept a celebrated journal.

Delacroix championed colour, movement and passionate feeling over the line-based classicism of Ingres. He was a master of vibrant juxtaposed colours that intensify each other, a lesson taken up by the Impressionists and Post-Impressionists, and his subjects came from literature, history, politics and the 'Orient'. Baudelaire praised him as the greatest painter of the age. Cézanne, Van Gogh and Matisse all acknowledged his influence.

name: Jean-François Millet
bio: A founder of the Barbizon school who gave peasant labour a solemn dignity. Van Gogh copied his work repeatedly.
bio_full: Jean-François Millet was born into a peasant farming family in the hamlet of Gruchy on the Normandy coast. He studied in Cherbourg and in Paris with Paul Delaroche, and supported himself for years with portraits and small pastoral pictures. In 1849, fleeing revolution and cholera in Paris, he settled in the village of Barbizon on the edge of the Forest of Fontainebleau, where he lived for the rest of his life among a group of landscape painters. The Sower (1850) and The Angelus (1857–59) made his name, and he was awarded the Legion of Honour in 1868.

Millet depicted the labour of French peasants, sowing, reaping, gleaning and digging, with monumental, almost biblical dignity, simplified forms and earthy colour. Conservative critics accused him of socialism, while others saw his work as deeply religious. The Angelus became one of the most famous paintings in France and later obsessed Salvador Dalí. Van Gogh revered Millet and made many copies after his compositions.

name: Gustave Courbet
bio: The self-declared leader of Realism, Courbet painted ordinary people at the scale of history painting. He was exiled after his role in the Paris Commune.
bio_full: Gustave Courbet was born in Ornans in the Jura region to a prosperous farming family. He moved to Paris in 1839 and taught himself mostly by copying in the Louvre. After Dinner at Ornans won him a medal in 1849, and then The Stone Breakers (destroyed in 1945), A Burial at Ornans and other large paintings of rural life caused scandal at the Salon. When the 1855 World's Fair rejected some of his works, he built his own 'Pavilion of Realism' nearby and issued a Realist manifesto. A committed republican, he took part in the Paris Commune of 1871, was blamed for the toppling of the Vendôme Column, and was imprisoned and later ordered to pay for its reconstruction. He fled to Switzerland in 1873 and died in exile in 1877.

Courbet declared that painting should depict only 'real and existing things', and he refused to paint angels because he had never seen one. He gave peasants, labourers and provincial townspeople the monumental scale once reserved for history painting. He worked with thick paint, often applied with a palette knife, and painted landscapes, seascapes, hunting scenes and provocative nudes, including The Origin of the World (1866). He was a key precursor of Manet and modern art.

name: Édouard Manet
bio: Manet's flat, frank pictures of modern Paris caused scandal and paved the way for Impressionism. He is often seen as the first modern painter.
bio_full: Édouard Manet was born in Paris to a wealthy family; his father was a senior magistrate. After failing to enter the naval academy and sailing as a trainee to Rio de Janeiro, he studied for six years with the academic painter Thomas Couture. He admired Velázquez, Goya and Hals, and his early works show Spanish influence. Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe (1863) and Olympia (1865) caused huge scandals and made him the reluctant leader of young avant-garde painters who met at the Café Guerbois. Yet he never exhibited at the Impressionists' independent exhibitions, still hoping for official success at the Salon. He was a friend of Baudelaire, Zola and Mallarmé. His health declined from the effects of syphilis, and he died in 1883 at 51, shortly after a leg amputation.

Manet painted modern Paris life, its cafés, boulevards, racecourses and people, with flat areas of colour, strong contrasts, little traditional modelling and bold black, often reworking old-master compositions in contemporary dress. His frankness and his emphasis on the painted surface broke with academic tradition and are seen as the starting point of modern painting. His sister-in-law was the Impressionist Berthe Morisot.

name: Edgar Degas
bio: A founder of the Impressionist exhibitions who preferred the studio to the outdoors. He is known for dancers, racecourses and bold, cropped compositions influenced by photography and Japanese prints.
bio_full: Edgar Degas was born into a wealthy Parisian banking family. He abandoned law to study art, deeply admired Ingres, and spent 1856–59 in Italy copying the old masters. He began as a history painter and portraitist, as in The Bellelli Family. In 1872–73 he visited relatives in New Orleans and painted A Cotton Office. He was a central organiser of the Impressionist exhibitions and showed in seven of the eight, but disliked the label and painting outdoors, preferring to call himself a realist. In later life his eyesight declined. He held fiercely anti-Dreyfusard views, which ended several friendships. He died in Paris in 1917.

Degas observed modern Paris: ballet dancers in rehearsal, racehorses and jockeys, laundresses, milliners, café life and women bathing. He used asymmetrical, cropped compositions and unusual viewpoints inspired by photography and Japanese prints. He was an innovator in pastel, monotype and photography, and his wax sculptures, found in his studio after his death, were cast in bronze. He is one of the great draughtsmen of the 19th century.

name: Claude Monet
bio: The purest Impressionist, Monet painted the same motif in changing light in series such as haystacks, Rouen Cathedral and his water garden at Giverny.
bio_full: Claude Monet was born in Paris and grew up in Le Havre, where he made a name drawing caricatures. The landscape painter Eugène Boudin introduced him to painting outdoors. In Paris he met Renoir, Sisley and Bazille in Charles Gleyre's studio, and the friends developed painting directly from nature. He endured years of poverty with his companion and later wife Camille Doncieux, who died in 1879. He spent 1870–71 in London and then lived at Argenteuil on the Seine. He helped organise the first independent group exhibition in 1874, which gave Impressionism its name. From 1883 he lived at Giverny, where he created a flower garden and a water garden with a Japanese bridge. He married Alice Hoschedé in 1892.

Monet devoted his life to capturing fleeting light and atmosphere. From the 1890s he painted series of the same motif at different times of day and seasons, including Haystacks, Poplars, Rouen Cathedral, the Houses of Parliament in London and his water lilies. Despite cataracts, which were operated on in 1923, he worked on huge water lily paintings until his death in 1926, and these were later seen as forerunners of abstract art.

name: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
bio: Renoir's warm, dappled scenes of Parisians at leisure define the joyful side of Impressionism. He later turned toward a more classical, sculptural style.
bio_full: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was born in Limoges to a working-class family who moved to Paris. As a teenager he was an apprentice painter of porcelain. He studied in Gleyre's studio, where he befriended Monet, and the two painted side by side at the bathing spot of La Grenouillère in 1869. He exhibited at the early Impressionist shows and found patrons such as the publisher Georges Charpentier. After a trip to Italy in 1881 he turned to a harder, more linear style inspired by Raphael and Ingres, and later to warm, rounded figures. He married Aline Charigot in 1890. One son, Jean Renoir, became a great film director. Despite severe rheumatoid arthritis, he continued to paint into old age at Cagnes-sur-Mer, where he died in 1919.

Renoir is the painter of the joyful side of Impressionism: Parisians dancing, boating, picnicking and chatting in dappled sunlight, children, flowers and voluptuous nudes. He painted with soft, feathery brushwork and warm iridescent colour. In his last years he also made sculptures with the help of an assistant.

name: Berthe Morisot
bio: A core member of the Impressionist group who exhibited in nearly all its shows. Her feathery brushwork captured intimate domestic and women's lives.
bio_full: Berthe Morisot was born in Bourges, the daughter of a senior government official, and grew up in Paris. Women were not admitted to the École des Beaux-Arts, so she and her sister Edma studied privately, copying in the Louvre and learning from Camille Corot. She met Édouard Manet in 1868 and posed for several of his paintings, including The Balcony. In 1874 she married Manet's brother Eugène, and she exhibited at the first Impressionist exhibition the same year. She showed at all but one of the eight exhibitions, missing only the year her daughter Julie was born. She died in 1895, aged 54, of pneumonia caught while nursing Julie.

Morisot painted the private world she knew: mothers and children, women dressing, reading and resting, gardens and seaside scenes. She worked with rapid, feathery, almost abstract brushstrokes and luminous whites, and her technique was among the most radical of the group. Long overshadowed by her male colleagues, she is now recognised as one of the core members of Impressionism.

name: Auguste Rodin
bio: The founder of modern sculpture, Rodin modelled restless, expressive surfaces and fragmentary figures. Many of his best-known works began as parts of The Gates of Hell.
bio_full: Auguste Rodin was born in Paris to a working-class family. He failed three times to enter the École des Beaux-Arts and spent years as a decorative craftsman, including six years in Belgium. A trip to Italy in 1875 to see Michelangelo transformed him. His first major statue, The Age of Bronze (1877), was so lifelike that critics accused him of casting it from a living model. In 1880 he was commissioned to make a monumental portal, The Gates of Hell, based on Dante. He worked on it for the rest of his life and generated many of his independent sculptures from it. His other major works include The Burghers of Calais and the Monument to Balzac, which was rejected by its commissioners in 1898. His pupil and lover Camille Claudel was a brilliant sculptor in her own right. He donated his works to the state, and his Paris residence, the Hôtel Biron, opened as the Musée Rodin in 1919.

Rodin is considered the father of modern sculpture. He modelled clay with rough, expressive, light-catching surfaces, made fragments and partial figures into finished works, and reused and recombined forms. His sculptures convey intense inner emotion and physical energy, and his influence on Brâncuși, Matisse and later sculptors was enormous.

name: Paul Cézanne
bio: Cézanne rebuilt nature from planes of colour and multiple viewpoints. Picasso and Matisse both called him the father of modern art.
bio_full: Paul Cézanne was born in Aix-en-Provence, the son of a prosperous banker. At school he became close friends with the future novelist Émile Zola, who encouraged him to go to Paris in 1861. His early works are dark and violent, and they were repeatedly rejected by the Salon. Under Pissarro's guidance in Pontoise in the early 1870s he brightened his palette and showed at the first and third Impressionist exhibitions. He then withdrew increasingly to Provence. His friendship with Zola ended in 1886 after Zola's novel L'Œuvre portrayed a failed painter apparently modelled on him. In 1895 the dealer Ambroise Vollard gave him his first solo exhibition, and young artists began to make pilgrimages to Aix. He died in 1906 after being caught in a storm while painting outdoors.

Cézanne aimed to 'make of Impressionism something solid and durable, like the art of the museums'. He built his paintings from patches of colour that model form, combined multiple viewpoints in a single image, and simplified nature into geometric structures. In a letter he advised treating nature through 'the cylinder, the sphere, the cone'. His still lifes, portraits, bathers and landscapes of Provence paved the way for Cubism and abstraction. Picasso and Matisse both called him 'the father of us all'.

name: Paul Gauguin
bio: A former stockbroker who pursued 'primitive' simplicity in Brittany and then French Polynesia. His flat, symbolic colour influenced Symbolists and Fauves; his colonial gaze is debated today.
bio_full: Paul Gauguin was born in Paris and spent part of his childhood in Lima, Peru, with his mother's family. After serving in the merchant navy and the navy, he became a successful stockbroker, married the Danish Mette Gad and had five children. He collected Impressionist paintings and began painting as an amateur under Pissarro, exhibiting in the Impressionist shows. After the stock market crash of 1882 he decided to paint full time, and his family life collapsed. He worked in Brittany at Pont-Aven, in Martinique and, briefly and disastrously, with Van Gogh in Arles in 1888. In search of an unspoiled 'primitive' paradise he went to Tahiti in 1891, returned to France, and left again in 1895. He spent his last years in the Marquesas Islands, where he died in 1903, in conflict with the colonial authorities and the Church.

Gauguin developed a style of flat areas of bold, non-naturalistic colour enclosed by dark outlines, influenced by Japanese prints, stained glass and folk art. His aim was to express ideas, emotions and spiritual meaning rather than to record appearances. He was also an innovative woodcut artist and sculptor and a crucial influence on the Nabis, Fauvism and Expressionism. Today his colonial fantasy and his sexual relationships with very young Tahitian girls are the subject of critical debate, often discussed alongside his art.

name: Vincent van Gogh
bio: In a career of about ten years Van Gogh made some 2,100 works, using vivid colour and rhythmic brushstrokes to express emotion. He sold very little in his lifetime and became one of the most famous artists in history.
bio_full: Vincent van Gogh was born in Zundert in the southern Netherlands, the son of a Protestant pastor. He worked for the international art dealers Goupil & Cie in The Hague, London and Paris, then as a teacher and lay preacher, including among miners in the Borinage region of Belgium. In 1880, aged 27, he decided to become an artist, largely self-taught and supported by his younger brother Theo, an art dealer. After dark, earthy works such as The Potato Eaters (1885), he moved to Paris in 1886, where he discovered Impressionism and Japanese prints. In February 1888 he moved to Arles in Provence, dreaming of an artists' colony. Gauguin's stay there ended in December 1888 with a crisis in which Van Gogh cut off part of his own ear. He spent a year as a voluntary patient in an asylum at Saint-Rémy. In May 1890 he moved to Auvers-sur-Oise near Paris, where he shot himself in July and died two days later, aged 37.

In a career of about ten years Van Gogh produced around 860 oil paintings and more than 1,200 drawings and watercolours, most in his last two years. His vivid colour, thick paint and swirling, rhythmic brushstrokes express intense emotion, and he became a central influence on Expressionism. He sold very little during his lifetime. His more than 800 surviving letters, most to Theo, are among the most moving documents of any artist's life. Theo's widow, Jo van Gogh-Bonger, worked tirelessly to make his work known.
