name: Georges Seurat
bio: Seurat developed Pointillism, building images from small dots of pure colour based on optical theory. He died at 31.
bio_full: Georges Seurat was born in Paris to a well-off family. He studied at the École des Beaux-Arts with Henri Lehmann, a pupil of Ingres, and absorbed scientific theories of colour by Michel-Eugène Chevreul and Ogden Rood. He also made remarkable velvety drawings in black conté crayon. When the Salon rejected his Bathers at Asnières in 1884, he helped found the Society of Independent Artists. He showed A Sunday on La Grande Jatte at the last Impressionist exhibition in 1886, where the critic Félix Fénéon coined the term Neo-Impressionism. With Paul Signac he led a group of followers. He died suddenly in 1891, aged 31, probably of an infection, leaving a secret partner, Madeleine Knobloch, and their infant son.

Seurat developed a technique, later called Pointillism or Divisionism, of placing small dots or strokes of pure colour side by side so that they would mix in the viewer's eye, aiming at greater luminosity than mixed paint. His carefully planned, almost geometric compositions and stiff, stylised figures brought order and science to Impressionism's spontaneity, and they influenced Fauvism, Futurism and abstract art.

name: Gustav Klimt
bio: Co-founder and first president of the Vienna Secession. His 'golden phase' combined gold leaf, ornament and erotic symbolism.
bio_full: Gustav Klimt was born in Baumgarten near Vienna, the son of a gold engraver. He studied at the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts and, with his brother Ernst and Franz Matsch, formed a successful firm decorating public buildings, including the Burgtheater and the Kunsthistorisches Museum. In 1897 he led a group of young artists who broke away from the conservative establishment to found the Vienna Secession, and he became its first president. His ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna were attacked as pornographic and were later destroyed by fire in 1945. He spent summers at the Attersee painting landscapes with his lifelong companion, the fashion designer Emilie Flöge. He died in 1918 after a stroke, during the influenza pandemic.

Klimt's 'golden phase', influenced partly by the Byzantine mosaics he saw in Ravenna in 1903, combined realistically painted faces and hands with flat, ornamental surfaces of gold leaf and pattern. His themes were love, sexuality, life and death, and the female body. He was a central figure of Viennese Art Nouveau (Jugendstil) and mentored the young Egon Schiele. He also made thousands of erotic drawings.

name: Edvard Munch
bio: Munch turned anxiety, love and death into charged images of colour and line. He was a crucial forerunner of German Expressionism.
bio_full: Edvard Munch was born in Løten, Norway, and grew up in Kristiania (now Oslo), the son of a devout army doctor. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five, and his favourite sister Sophie when he was 13, and illness, death and anxiety haunted his work. He joined the bohemian circle of Kristiania, studied in Paris, and in 1892 an exhibition of his work in Berlin was closed after a scandal, which made him famous in Germany. In the 1890s he developed his cycle of paintings The Frieze of Life, on love, anxiety and death. After a breakdown in 1908 and treatment in a Copenhagen clinic, his art became brighter. He painted murals for the Oslo University aula and lived at Ekely outside Oslo. The Nazis declared his work 'degenerate'. He died in January 1944 and left his remaining works to the city of Oslo, now in the Munch Museum.

Munch used simplified, flowing forms, symbolic colour and expressive distortion to depict inner psychological states. He was also a hugely innovative printmaker in woodcut and lithography. A crucial bridge between Symbolism and Expressionism, he is Norway's most famous artist.

name: Henri Matisse
bio: Leader of the Fauves and, with Picasso, the defining artist of early modernism. In old age he made radiant cut-paper compositions.
bio_full: Henri Matisse was born in Le Cateau-Cambrésis in northern France and trained as a lawyer. He began painting in 1889 while recovering from appendicitis, when his mother gave him a box of paints. He studied in Paris in the studio of the Symbolist painter Gustave Moreau. In the summer of 1905, working at Collioure with André Derain, he developed the explosive colour that led critics to call them the Fauves ('wild beasts'). Collectors including Gertrude and Leo Stein and the Russian Sergei Shchukin supported him. From 1917 he spent most of his time in Nice. After surgery for cancer in 1941 he was often confined to bed or a wheelchair. He then invented a new art of painted paper cut-outs, as in the book Jazz (1947), and designed the Chapel of the Rosary at Vence (1948–51). He died in Nice in 1954.

With Picasso, Matisse was the defining artist of early modernism. He used pure, expressive colour, simplified drawing and flattened space to create works of balance, joy and decorative harmony. He once said he dreamed of an art like a good armchair, offering rest to the tired mind. He worked in painting, sculpture, printmaking, book design and cut paper, and his influence on abstraction, colour field painting and design is incalculable.

name: Pablo Picasso
bio: The most influential artist of the 20th century, co-inventor of Cubism and endlessly reinventive across painting, sculpture, ceramics and print.
bio_full: Pablo Picasso was born in Málaga, the son of the painter and drawing teacher José Ruiz Blasco. He grew up in A Coruña and Barcelona, where he was a child prodigy. He settled in Paris in 1904. After the melancholy Blue Period (1901–04), triggered partly by the suicide of his friend Carles Casagemas, and the Rose Period of circus performers, he painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907). With Georges Braque he then invented Cubism and collage. He designed for the Ballets Russes, married the dancer Olga Khokhlova, passed through a Neoclassical phase and joined the margins of Surrealism. His mural Guernica (1937) became a universal anti-war image. He stayed in Paris during the German occupation, joined the French Communist Party in 1944, and later lived in the south of France, working in ceramics at Vallauris. He died at Mougins in 1973, aged 91.

Picasso is the most influential artist of the 20th century. He constantly reinvented his style and worked in painting, sculpture, printmaking, ceramics, stage design and assemblage, producing an estimated tens of thousands of works. His tumultuous relationships with a succession of women, including Marie-Thérèse Walter, Dora Maar, Françoise Gilot and Jacqueline Roque, shaped his art and are now critically examined. Museums dedicated to him exist in Paris, Barcelona, Málaga and Antibes.

name: Georges Braque
bio: Braque developed Cubism side by side with Picasso between 1908 and 1914 and introduced papier collé (pasted paper).
bio_full: Georges Braque was born in Argenteuil and grew up in Le Havre, training like his father and grandfather as a decorative house painter. In Paris he joined the Fauves in 1906–07. Meeting Picasso and seeing Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, together with the 1907 Cézanne retrospective, transformed his work. His landscapes of L'Estaque (1908) led a critic to speak of 'little cubes', and from 1909 to 1914 he and Picasso developed Cubism so closely together that their works can be hard to tell apart. Braque compared them to mountaineers roped together. Braque invented papier collé (pasted paper) in 1912 and introduced stencilled letters, imitation wood grain and sand into painting. Badly wounded in the head in 1915, he recovered slowly and went on to develop a calmer, more lyrical style.

Braque's later still lifes, his series of Studio interiors and his images of birds are meditative explorations of space and texture. In 1953 he painted the ceiling of the Henri II room in the Louvre. In 1961 he became the first living artist to have a retrospective at the Louvre, and he received a state funeral in 1963.

name: Wassily Kandinsky
bio: A pioneer of abstract painting who compared colour to music. He co-founded Der Blaue Reiter and taught at the Bauhaus.
bio_full: Wassily Kandinsky was born in Moscow and trained in law and economics, becoming a lecturer at Moscow University. He recalled being overwhelmed by one of Monet's Haystacks at an 1896 exhibition and by a performance of Wagner's Lohengrin. At 30 he gave up his academic career and moved to Munich to study painting. With Gabriele Münter he painted in the Bavarian village of Murnau. In 1911 he published Concerning the Spiritual in Art and founded the Blue Rider (Der Blaue Reiter) group with Franz Marc. He returned to Russia during the First World War and the Revolution, then taught at the Bauhaus in Germany from 1922 to 1933, publishing Point and Line to Plane (1926). When the Nazis closed the Bauhaus he moved to Neuilly-sur-Seine near Paris, where he died in 1944.

Kandinsky was one of the pioneers of abstract painting. He believed colour and form could act directly on the soul like music, and he grouped his works as Impressions, Improvisations and Compositions, terms borrowed from music. His style moved from the expressive, colourful abstractions of the Munich years to the geometric forms of the Bauhaus period and the biomorphic, playful works of his last decade in Paris.

name: Piet Mondrian
bio: A founder of De Stijl, Mondrian reduced painting to black lines, white ground and primary colours in search of universal harmony.
bio_full: Piet Mondriaan (later Mondrian) was born in Amersfoort to a strict Calvinist family and trained at the Amsterdam Academy, first painting landscapes in the tradition of the Hague School. He was drawn to Theosophy and its search for universal spiritual truths. Moving to Paris in 1911, he discovered Cubism, and his series of trees became increasingly abstract. Trapped in the Netherlands during the First World War, he co-founded the movement and magazine De Stijl ('The Style') with Theo van Doesburg in 1917. He split from van Doesburg in the 1920s, reportedly over the use of diagonals. He lived in Paris until 1938, then London, and from 1940 New York, where he died in 1944.

From around 1920 Mondrian developed what he called Neoplasticism: a pure, universal art reduced to straight horizontal and vertical lines, the three primary colours and the non-colours black, white and grey, in perfect asymmetrical balance. He believed this abstract harmony could point the way to a harmonious society. His style has had an enormous influence on architecture, graphic design, fashion and furniture design.

name: Marcel Duchamp
bio: Duchamp's 'readymades' — ordinary objects declared art — shifted art from the eye to the idea. He is a founding figure of conceptual art.
bio_full: Marcel Duchamp was born in Blainville-Crevon in Normandy into an artistic family: his brothers Jacques Villon and Raymond Duchamp-Villon and his sister Suzanne were also artists. His Cubist painting Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2 was withdrawn from a Paris exhibition in 1912 at the request of fellow Cubists, but it caused a sensation at the 1913 Armory Show in New York. Soon after, he gave up conventional painting and began making readymades, everyday objects selected and presented as art. He moved to New York in 1915 and worked for years on The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even (The Large Glass). He devoted much of his time to chess, playing for France in international tournaments, and created a female alter ego, Rrose Sélavy. He became an American citizen in 1955. After his death in 1968 it was discovered that he had spent 20 years secretly building a final work, Étant donnés, now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Duchamp rejected what he called 'retinal' art, made to please the eye, in favour of art addressed to the mind. His readymades, his puns and his idea that the artist's choice and context make something art laid the foundations of Dada, Pop Art, Conceptual Art and much contemporary art.

name: René Magritte
bio: A Surrealist who painted ordinary objects with deadpan clarity in impossible combinations, questioning how images and words relate to reality.
bio_full: René Magritte was born in Lessines in Belgium. His mother died when he was 13. He studied at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels and worked in a wallpaper factory and as a commercial and poster designer. Influenced by Giorgio de Chirico, he painted his first Surrealist work, The Lost Jockey, in 1926. From 1927 to 1930 he lived near Paris and took part in the Surrealist group around André Breton, but fell out with Breton and returned to Brussels, where he spent the rest of his life with his wife Georgette. He briefly experimented with a deliberately crude 'vache' style and an Impressionist-like style in the 1940s, then returned to his classic manner. He died in Brussels in 1967.

Magritte painted ordinary objects, such as bowler hats, apples, pipes, clouds, windows and curtains, with a precise, impersonal technique, but placed them in impossible combinations, scales and contexts. His aim was to make the familiar strange and to question the relationship between images, words and reality. His images have been endlessly adopted by advertising, album covers and film, and influenced Pop and Conceptual Art.

name: Salvador Dalí
bio: The most famous Surrealist, known for meticulously painted dreamscapes and a flamboyant public persona.
bio_full: Salvador Dalí was born in Figueres, Catalonia, into a prosperous family. An older brother, also named Salvador, had died before he was born, and Dalí later claimed this haunted him. He studied in Madrid, where he befriended the poet Federico García Lorca and the filmmaker Luis Buñuel, with whom he made the Surrealist film Un Chien Andalou (1929). In 1929 he met Gala, who became his muse, wife and manager, and he joined the Surrealist group in Paris. He was later expelled by André Breton for his politics and commercialism. He spent the years 1940–48 in the United States, where he became a celebrity, designed a dream sequence for Hitchcock's Spellbound and worked with Disney. He returned to Catalonia, living at Port Lligat. He created the Dalí Theatre-Museum in Figueres, which opened in 1974 and where he is buried. He died in 1989.

Dalí developed what he called the 'paranoiac-critical method', a way of tapping irrational associations and double images. He painted his hallucinatory dreamscapes with meticulous, old-master precision. Later he turned to religious, scientific and 'nuclear mysticism' subjects. His flamboyant persona, upturned moustache and showmanship made him one of the most famous artists of the 20th century.

name: Frida Kahlo
bio: Kahlo's intense self-portraits draw on Mexican folk art, her physical suffering and her identity. The Surrealists claimed her, though she rejected the label.
bio_full: Frida Kahlo was born in Coyoacán, Mexico City, in the 'Blue House' (Casa Azul), the daughter of a German-born photographer and a Mexican mother of mixed Indigenous and Spanish descent. She contracted polio at six, and at 18 she was gravely injured in a bus accident that broke her spine and pelvis and left her in pain for the rest of her life. She began painting while confined to bed, using a mirror fixed above her. In 1929 she married the muralist Diego Rivera. They divorced in 1939 and remarried in 1940. She lived in the United States in the early 1930s, and in 1939 the Louvre bought her painting The Frame. She taught at the La Esmeralda art school, and her first solo exhibition in Mexico, in 1953, she attended in her bed. She died in 1954, aged 47.

Kahlo painted around 200 works, about a third of them self-portraits, combining Mexican folk art, ex-voto paintings and pre-Columbian imagery with her own experiences of pain, love, the body, miscarriage and identity. André Breton claimed her as a Surrealist, but she said she painted her own reality, not dreams. Since the 1980s she has become a global icon of Mexican identity and feminism. Her house is a museum, and in Mexico her works are protected as national artistic monuments.

name: Edward Hopper
bio: Hopper painted American cities, diners and roadsides with stark light and a mood of loneliness.
bio_full: Edward Hopper was born in Nyack, New York, and studied illustration and painting at the New York School of Art under Robert Henri. He made three trips to Paris between 1906 and 1910 but remained largely untouched by the avant-garde. For years he earned his living as a commercial illustrator. He sold a painting at the 1913 Armory Show and made a series of etchings, but real success came only with a 1924 exhibition of watercolours. That year he married the painter Josephine Nivison, who managed his records and was his only model for female figures. His House by the Railroad was the first painting acquired by the new Museum of Modern Art in 1930. He spent summers on Cape Cod and lived in a studio on Washington Square in New York until his death in 1967.

Hopper painted American cities, diners, offices, hotel rooms, theatres, gas stations and empty streets, as well as New England houses and lighthouses. His clear, simplified forms, strong light and shadow, and isolated figures convey a mood of silence and loneliness that has profoundly influenced film, photography and the popular image of modern America.

name: Jackson Pollock
bio: Pollock poured and dripped paint onto canvas laid on the floor, making the act of painting the subject. He died in a car crash at 44.
bio_full: Paul Jackson Pollock was born in Cody, Wyoming, and grew up in Arizona and California. In New York he studied with the Regionalist Thomas Hart Benton at the Art Students League, worked for the government-funded Federal Art Project during the Depression, and attended an experimental workshop run by the Mexican muralist David Alfaro Siqueiros. He struggled with alcoholism all his life. In 1943 the collector Peggy Guggenheim gave him a contract and commissioned a large mural. In 1945 he married the painter Lee Krasner, and they moved to a farmhouse in Springs, Long Island, where his drip paintings developed between 1947 and 1950. In 1949 Life magazine asked whether he was the greatest living painter in the United States. He died in a car crash in August 1956, aged 44.

Pollock laid canvases on the floor and poured, dripped and flung paint from sticks, hardened brushes and cans, moving around and into the work. The finished paintings are dense, all-over webs of line without a central focus. Photographs and a film of him at work by Hans Namuth made the act of painting itself famous and shaped the idea of 'action painting'. He became the emblematic figure of Abstract Expressionism.

name: Mark Rothko
bio: A leading Colour Field painter whose soft-edged rectangles of colour aim at contemplative, almost religious experience.
bio_full: Mark Rothko was born Markus Rothkowitz in Dvinsk (now Daugavpils, Latvia), in the Russian Empire, to a Jewish family. In 1913 the family emigrated to Portland, Oregon. He won a scholarship to Yale but left without graduating, moved to New York and studied art. In the 1940s he painted mythological, Surrealist-influenced images, then 'multiforms' of soft colour patches. From around 1949 he arrived at his classic format: two or three soft-edged rectangles of luminous colour floating on a coloured field. In 1958–59 he painted a series of dark murals for the Four Seasons restaurant in the Seagram Building, then withdrew from the commission and gave some of the paintings to Tate. He later painted the murals for Harvard and the Rothko Chapel in Houston. Suffering from depression and ill health, he took his own life in his New York studio in February 1970.

Rothko rejected being called a colourist or an abstract artist. He said he was interested only in expressing basic human emotions such as tragedy, ecstasy and doom, and he wanted viewers to stand close to his large canvases and be enveloped by them. He became one of the leading figures of Colour Field painting and Abstract Expressionism.

name: Andy Warhol
bio: The leading figure of Pop Art, Warhol used silkscreen to mass-produce images of consumer goods and celebrities from his studio, the Factory.
bio_full: Andy Warhol was born Andrew Warhola in Pittsburgh, the son of Carpatho-Rusyn immigrants from present-day Slovakia. As a sickly child he spent long periods in bed drawing and collecting pictures of film stars. He studied commercial art at the Carnegie Institute of Technology and moved to New York in 1949, where he became a highly successful illustrator, especially of shoe advertisements. In 1962 his exhibition of Campbell's Soup Can paintings in Los Angeles and his Marilyn Monroe and Coca-Cola silkscreens made him the leading figure of Pop Art. His studio, the Factory, became a celebrated hub of artists, musicians, actors and hangers-on. He made experimental films, managed the rock band The Velvet Underground and founded Interview magazine. In 1968 he was shot and severely wounded by the writer Valerie Solanas. In the 1980s he collaborated with Jean-Michel Basquiat. He died in 1987 after routine gallbladder surgery.

Warhol erased the boundary between fine art, commerce and celebrity. He used commercial silkscreen printing and assistants to mass-produce images of consumer products, film stars, disasters and political figures, exploring fame, repetition, death and the media. He famously predicted that in the future everyone would be world-famous for 15 minutes. The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh opened in 1994.

name: Roy Lichtenstein
bio: Lichtenstein enlarged comic-strip panels with hand-painted Ben-Day dots, parodying mass-media images and painterly heroics.
bio_full: Roy Lichtenstein was born in New York City and studied art at Ohio State University, interrupted by army service in Europe during the Second World War. He taught at universities in Ohio and New York, painting in Abstract Expressionist and other styles. In 1961, according to the story, his son challenged him to paint as well as a Mickey Mouse comic book, and he painted Look Mickey, based on a cartoon. His 1962 exhibition at Leo Castelli's gallery made him famous. He went on to parody art history and Abstract Expressionism itself in series such as Brushstrokes, Mirrors, Entablatures and Artist's Studio, and he made sculpture and public art. He died in New York in 1997.

Lichtenstein took images from comic strips and advertisements and repainted them on a huge scale with thick black outlines, flat primary colours and hand-painted Ben-Day dots imitating cheap commercial printing. His work raised questions about originality, mass media and taste. Some of the comic artists whose panels he adapted have argued that their contribution has been underappreciated.

name: Myron
bio: A bronze sculptor of the early Classical period, active in Athens,, admired for capturing athletes in motion. None of his originals survive; his work is known through Roman marble copies.
bio_full: Myron was a bronze sculptor working in Athens in the decades around 470–440 BC. This was the 'Severe' or early Classical phase, when Greek sculpture was moving away from stiff archaic poses. Ancient tradition says he trained under Ageladas of Argos, who also taught Polykleitos. His most celebrated works were athletes and animals. Many ancient poems praise a bronze cow by him that was supposedly so lifelike that calves tried to suckle it and herdsmen tried to drive it off.

None of Myron's originals survive, so he is known through Roman marble copies and the remarks of writers such as Pliny the Elder. Pliny admired his range and rhythm but said he paid less attention to the expression of feeling. Myron's achievement was to capture a body at the instant of greatest action while keeping it balanced and calm. That idea runs through Western sculpture from the Renaissance to the Olympic imagery of the modern age.

name: Phidias
bio: The most famous sculptor of Classical Athens, who supervised the sculptural programme of the Parthenon under Pericles. His colossal gold-and-ivory statues of Athena and Zeus are lost.
bio_full: Phidias (Pheidias) was the most famous artist of Classical Athens. His friend the statesman Pericles put him in charge of the artistic programme on the Acropolis after the Persian Wars. He oversaw the sculpture of the Parthenon and made its cult statue, the Athena Parthenos, a figure about 12 metres high built of gold and ivory over a wooden core. He later made the colossal seated Zeus at Olympia, counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Excavators at Olympia found his workshop, including a cup scratched with the words 'I belong to Pheidias'.

Ancient sources say Phidias was accused of embezzling gold or of impiety, and his last years are obscure. All of his famous cult statues are lost and are known only from descriptions, coins and small copies. Even so, the Parthenon sculptures made under his direction became the standard of 'classical' beauty: calm, idealised and full of life. Through Renaissance and Neoclassical artists, his style shaped how the West imagined Greek art.

name: Polykleitos
bio: A bronze sculptor who wrote the Canon, a treatise on ideal human proportion. His relaxed, weight-shifted stance (contrapposto) became a model for Western sculpture.
bio_full: Polykleitos ran a leading bronze workshop in Argos in the Peloponnese in the second half of the 5th century BC and taught a whole school of followers. He was famous for statues of victorious athletes, such as the Diadoumenos (a youth tying a victory ribbon round his head), and for a gold-and-ivory statue of Hera at Argos that ancient visitors ranked alongside Phidias's work.

His lasting influence came from his treatise, the Canon. It set out a system of ideal proportions in which every part of the body relates to every other by measured ratios (symmetria). He illustrated it with a statue, generally identified as the Doryphoros. The treatise is lost, but its ideas passed through Roman writers such as Vitruvius to the Renaissance, where Leonardo's Vitruvian Man takes up the same search for perfect human proportion.

name: Praxiteles
bio: The leading Athenian sculptor of the 4th century BC, known for softer, more sensuous marble figures. He made the first monumental fully nude statue of a goddess.
bio_full: Praxiteles was the leading Athenian sculptor of the mid-4th century BC and probably the son of the sculptor Kephisodotos. He worked mainly in marble and had it delicately painted. He moved away from the grandeur of the Parthenon generation towards softer, more relaxed and sensuous figures, often in an S-shaped pose that leans on a support. His works included the Apollo Sauroktonos (Apollo the Lizard-Slayer). A Hermes holding the infant Dionysus, found at Olympia in 1877, is often attributed to him, though scholars still debate whether it is his original.

Ancient writers linked him romantically with the celebrated courtesan Phryne, said to be the model for his Aphrodite. His gentle, intimate approach to the gods reshaped Hellenistic and Roman taste and, through Roman copies, the Renaissance ideal of the female nude.

name: Agesander, Athenodoros & Polydorus
bio: Three sculptors from Rhodes named by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder as the makers of the Laocoön group. Their exact dates and whether the work is an original or a copy are debated.
bio_full: Agesander, Athenodoros and Polydorus were sculptors from the island of Rhodes, a major centre of late Hellenistic sculpture. We know them almost entirely through Pliny the Elder, who named them as the makers of the Laocoön group in the palace of the emperor Titus and called it a work superior to all others in painting or bronze. Their names also appear on the sculptures found in 1957 in the grotto of the emperor Tiberius's villa at Sperlonga, which show episodes from the Odyssey.

Whether the Laocoön is a Hellenistic original of about 200 BC, a Roman copy of a bronze, or a new work made for Roman patrons in the 1st century BC or AD is still debated. Its writhing, theatrical style is the high point of the 'Hellenistic baroque', and its rediscovery in 1506 had an enormous effect on Michelangelo and later artists.

name: Cimabue
bio: A Florentine painter who began loosening Byzantine conventions toward greater naturalism. Tradition makes him Giotto's teacher.
bio_full: Cenni di Pepo, called Cimabue, was born in Florence around 1240 and is the earliest Florentine painter whose name is attached to major surviving works. He worked in Rome, at Assisi (where he painted frescoes in the Upper Church of San Francesco) and in Pisa, where he made the mosaic of St John in the cathedral apse shortly before his death. Tradition, followed by Vasari, makes him Giotto's teacher.

Cimabue still worked within the Byzantine 'Greek manner', with gold grounds and stylised drapery. He gave it new weight, emotion and a sense of real space, so his figures begin to feel like bodies rather than icons. Dante paid him an ambiguous tribute in Purgatory: 'Cimabue thought he held the field in painting, and now Giotto has the cry.' His great painted Crucifix in Santa Croce, badly damaged in the 1966 Florence flood, became a symbol of the city's lost heritage.

name: Duccio di Buoninsegna
bio: The founder of the Sienese school, combining Byzantine elegance and gold with new tenderness and narrative clarity.
bio_full: Duccio di Buoninsegna was the founding master of Sienese painting. He is first documented in 1278 and died around 1319. In 1285 he received the commission for the huge Rucellai Madonna for the Florentine church of Santa Maria Novella, now in the Uffizi. That a Sienese painter won a Florentine commission shows how high his reputation stood. Records suggest he was often fined and in debt, but his workshop shaped Sienese art for generations, through pupils such as Simone Martini and the Lorenzetti brothers.

Duccio kept the gold, line and elegance of Byzantine painting but added warmth, tender human gesture and clear, lively storytelling in small narrative scenes. Where Florentine painting after Giotto stressed sculptural mass, the Sienese tradition he founded valued colour, grace and lyrical detail. That contrast ran through Italian painting for the rest of the Gothic age.

name: Lorenzo Ghiberti
bio: A goldsmith and sculptor who won the 1401 competition for the Florence Baptistery doors, a contest often taken as the start of the Renaissance. He spent most of his life on two sets of bronze doors.
bio_full: Lorenzo Ghiberti trained as a goldsmith. In 1401, at about 23, he won the competition to make the second set of bronze doors for the Florence Baptistery, beating Filippo Brunelleschi among others. Both trial panels, showing the Sacrifice of Isaac, survive in the Bargello. The doors with 28 scenes took him until 1424. He then spent most of the next three decades on a second pair, which Michelangelo reputedly called worthy to be the Gates of Paradise.

Ghiberti's workshop was a training ground for the next generation, including Donatello, Michelozzo and Paolo Uccello. He also wrote the Commentarii, which contains the first autobiography by a European artist and an early history of Italian art. His work bridges the graceful International Gothic style and the new Renaissance interest in perspective, classical architecture and the nude.

name: Filippo Brunelleschi
bio: Architect and engineer credited with the first systematic demonstration of linear perspective. His dome for Florence Cathedral was an engineering feat without precedent since antiquity.
bio_full: Filippo Brunelleschi was trained as a goldsmith. After losing the 1401 Baptistery doors competition to Ghiberti, he turned increasingly to architecture and engineering. Tradition says he went to Rome with Donatello to measure and study the ancient ruins. Around 1415–20 he made a celebrated experiment with painted panels of the Baptistery and a mirror. It demonstrated the rules of linear perspective, which the theorist Leon Battista Alberti soon codified for painters.

His buildings in Florence are the founding works of Renaissance architecture: the Ospedale degli Innocenti, the churches of San Lorenzo and Santo Spirito, and the Pazzi Chapel. They are built from clear, mathematically related proportions, round arches and classical columns in grey pietra serena stone against white walls. His crowning achievement was the cathedral dome, and he was given the rare honour of burial inside the cathedral itself.

name: Masaccio
bio: In a career of barely six years, Masaccio applied perspective and solid, light-modelled figures to painting. He died at 26.
bio_full: Tommaso di Ser Giovanni, nicknamed Masaccio ('clumsy' or 'big Tom'), joined the Florentine painters' guild in 1422. He worked alongside the older painter Masolino, most famously on the Brancacci Chapel frescoes in Santa Maria del Carmine. He also painted the Pisa Polyptych of 1426, now divided among several museums. He went to Rome around 1428 and died there at only 26, in circumstances that remain unclear.

In barely six years Masaccio did for painting what Brunelleschi did for architecture and Donatello for sculpture. He gave figures real weight under a single consistent light, used scientific perspective, and showed emotion with sober dignity. Vasari wrote that the Brancacci Chapel became a school for later artists. The young Michelangelo copied its figures, and a fist fight there with a rival is said to have broken his nose.

name: Fra Angelico
bio: A Dominican friar-painter who combined Renaissance space with serene devotional clarity, notably in the cells of the convent of San Marco.
bio_full: Born Guido di Pietro in the Mugello near Florence, he became a Dominican friar at Fiesole in the 1420s, taking the name Fra Giovanni. He was soon called 'Angelico' for the devotion of his painting and his life, and he was officially beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1982. When Cosimo de' Medici paid for the rebuilding of the convent of San Marco in Florence, Fra Angelico and his assistants frescoed the chapter house, corridors and the friars' cells. He later worked in Rome for Popes Eugenius IV and Nicholas V and decorated the Niccoline Chapel in the Vatican.

Fra Angelico combined the new Renaissance tools of perspective, solid figures and real light with a serene, luminous colour and clarity suited to prayer. The cell frescoes at San Marco are deliberately sparse so they could aid a friar's meditation, but his altarpieces are rich with gold and colour. He was one of the most admired painters in Italy in his lifetime.

name: Piero della Francesca
bio: A painter and mathematician whose works have a calm, geometric order and cool light. He wrote treatises on perspective and geometry.
bio_full: Piero della Francesca spent much of his life in his small home town of Borgo San Sepolcro in Tuscany, but worked for the courts of Rimini, Ferrara and above all Urbino. In Urbino he painted the famous profile portraits of Duke Federico da Montefeltro and his wife Battista Sforza (Uffizi). His masterpiece in fresco is the Legend of the True Cross in the church of San Francesco at Arezzo. He also painted the Resurrection in Sansepolcro, which Aldous Huxley called 'the best picture in the world'.

Piero was also a serious mathematician. He wrote treatises on perspective (De prospectiva pingendi), arithmetic and the five regular solids, and his paintings have a still, geometric calm, pale cool colour and a clear daylight. He was largely forgotten for centuries. 20th-century critics and artists rediscovered him and saw in his ordered forms an anticipation of Cézanne and modern abstraction.

name: Andrea Mantegna
bio: Court painter to the Gonzaga in Mantua, famous for archaeological detail and daring foreshortening.
bio_full: Andrea Mantegna was adopted as a boy by the Paduan painter and collector Francesco Squarcione. In Padua he absorbed the university city's passion for antiquity and Donatello's recent sculpture there. He set up independently while still a teenager and married Nicolosia Bellini, which made him brother-in-law to Giovanni Bellini. His early frescoes in the Ovetari Chapel in the Eremitani church were largely destroyed by bombing in 1944. From 1460 until his death he was court painter to the Gonzaga family in Mantua.

Mantegna was the most archaeological painter of the Renaissance, filling his scenes with accurately studied Roman architecture, inscriptions and armour. His figures can look as hard and sharp as carved stone. He was a master of steep perspective and foreshortening and an influential engraver, whose prints spread his style north of the Alps to artists such as Dürer. His series The Triumphs of Caesar is now at Hampton Court.

name: Giovanni Bellini
bio: The father of Venetian Renaissance painting, who pioneered oil technique in Venice and taught Giorgione and Titian. His landscapes glow with natural light.
bio_full: Giovanni Bellini came from Venice's leading family of painters: his father Jacopo and brother Gentile were also prominent artists. For around half a century he ran the city's most important workshop, painting altarpieces for its churches, devotional Madonnas and later portraits, including the Doge Leonardo Loredan (National Gallery, London). His pupils included Giorgione and Titian, and when Dürer visited Venice in 1506 he wrote that Bellini, though very old, was 'still the best in painting'.

Bellini was among the first Venetians to master oil paint. He used it to create soft, glowing light, warm atmosphere and landscapes that seem to carry the emotion of the sacred figures. His great altarpieces, such as the San Zaccaria Madonna of 1505, fuse figures and architecture in golden light. That move from line towards colour and atmosphere became the defining trait of Venetian painting.

name: Rogier van der Weyden
bio: City painter of Brussels and the most influential Netherlandish artist of his age, known for intense emotion and sculptural figures.
bio_full: Rogier de le Pasture, known in Flemish as Rogier van der Weyden, was born in Tournai. He trained there in the workshop of Robert Campin, whose robust realism he refined. By 1436 he was official painter to the city of Brussels, where he ran a large and influential workshop. He visited Italy, probably around the Jubilee of 1450, and worked for the Burgundian court, the Medici and the Este. His great polyptych of the Last Judgment still stands in the Hospices de Beaune.

Where van Eyck was the cool observer of light and texture, Rogier was the painter of emotion. His figures are elegant and sculptural, arranged in clear rhythmic compositions, and they express grief and devotion with intense, restrained feeling. His portraits of the Burgundian nobility set a model for courtly portraiture. Through his workshop and the many copies of his designs, he became the most widely imitated painter in northern Europe in the later 15th century.

name: Hans Holbein the Younger
bio: A brilliant portraitist who became painter to Henry VIII of England. His portraits combine precise likeness with display of status.
bio_full: Hans Holbein the Younger was the son of the Augsburg painter Hans Holbein the Elder. He settled in Basel, where he painted portraits of the scholar Erasmus and designed book illustrations, including his famous woodcut series the Dance of Death. As the Reformation disrupted religious commissions, he went to England in 1526 with an introduction from Erasmus to Sir Thomas More. He returned for good in 1532 and became King's Painter to Henry VIII, recording the king, his court, his wives and his ministers until his death in London in 1543, probably of plague.

Holbein's portraits combine extraordinary realism, cool unflattering observation of each face, with the brilliant depiction of rich clothes and objects that proclaimed status. His drawings, many now in the Royal Collection at Windsor, are among the finest portrait studies ever made. His lost mural of Henry VIII for Whitehall Palace, destroyed by fire in 1698, fixed the king's image, legs apart and fists on hips, for posterity.
