name: Giorgione
bio: A mysterious Venetian who pioneered poetic, mood-driven landscape painting. Only a handful of works are securely his; he died young, probably of plague.
bio_full: Very little is known for certain about Giorgione ('Big George'), born Giorgio da Castelfranco. He probably trained with Giovanni Bellini, became famous in Venice for poetic small paintings made for private collectors, and in 1508 painted frescoes, now almost entirely lost, on the façade of the German merchants' warehouse (the Fondaco dei Tedeschi) with the young Titian. He died of plague in 1510, still in his early thirties.

Only a handful of paintings are securely attributed to him, including The Tempest, The Three Philosophers in Vienna, and the Sleeping Venus in Dresden, which Titian finished. Yet his influence was immense. He made mood, landscape and atmosphere the true subjects of painting, often leaving the narrative deliberately mysterious, and he painted directly in oil without detailed preparatory drawing. The 'Giorgionesque' style of soft light and dreamy, enigmatic pastoral reshaped Venetian art.
portrait_file: Self portrait, by Giorgio da Castelfranco.jpg

name: Parmigianino
bio: A leading Mannerist known for elegant, elongated figures and virtuoso effects.
bio_full: Girolamo Francesco Maria Mazzola, called Parmigianino ('the little one from Parma'), was a prodigy. He went to Rome in 1524 to seek papal patronage, bringing his remarkable self-portrait in a convex mirror as a calling card. He was working there when imperial troops sacked the city in 1527, and he escaped to Bologna. Back in Parma he was commissioned to fresco the church of Santa Maria della Steccata, but he fell years behind, was briefly jailed for breach of contract, and died in 1540 at only 37. According to Vasari, he had become obsessed with alchemy.

Parmigianino is one of the defining artists of Mannerism. His figures are impossibly elegant, with elongated necks, hands and limbs, refined and self-consciously artificial, designed to dazzle the sophisticated viewer. He was also one of the first Italian painters to make etchings, and his many graceful drawings were eagerly collected.
portrait_file: Parmigianino Selfportrait.jpg
portrait_caption: Self-portrait in a Convex Mirror, c. 1524

name: Agnolo Bronzino
bio: Court painter to Cosimo I de' Medici, famed for cool, enamel-smooth portraits and complex allegories.
bio_full: Agnolo di Cosimo, called Bronzino, was the pupil and adopted son of the eccentric Florentine painter Jacopo Pontormo. He became court painter to Cosimo I de' Medici, Duke of Florence, and his wife Eleonora of Toledo, decorating Eleonora's chapel in the Palazzo Vecchio and producing official portraits of the ducal family. He was also a witty poet and a founding member of Florence's Accademia del Disegno in 1563.

Bronzino's portraits are the epitome of Mannerist court style. His sitters are cool and aloof, flawlessly smooth as if made of porcelain, and dressed in sumptuous fabrics rendered with jewel-like precision. Their emotional reserve expresses the rank and self-control expected at court. His allegories are intricate intellectual puzzles that mix eroticism with moralising.
portrait_file: Alessandro Allori, santissima trinità, 1567-1571 circa, ritratto dei maestri, bronzino (cropped).jpg
portrait_caption: Portrait in Alessandro Allori's Holy Trinity fresco, c. 1567–71

name: Tintoretto
bio: A fast, dramatic Venetian painter who aimed to combine 'the drawing of Michelangelo and the colour of Titian', with dynamic diagonals and theatrical light.
bio_full: Jacopo Robusti was nicknamed Tintoretto ('the little dyer') after his father's trade. He spent almost his entire life in Venice, where his speed and energy earned him the nickname 'il Furioso'. His greatest project was the decoration of the Scuola Grande di San Rocco, a religious confraternity's meeting house, which he filled with more than fifty paintings over some 23 years. He also painted the enormous Paradise in the Doge's Palace. His daughter Marietta and son Domenico worked in his busy studio.

Tintoretto reportedly aimed to combine 'the drawing of Michelangelo and the colour of Titian'. His paintings are full of drama, with plunging diagonals, sudden shifts of scale, theatrical lighting and figures in violent motion. He sometimes worked out compositions with small wax figures in model stages. His visionary religious painting influenced El Greco and anticipated the Baroque.
portrait_file: Tintoretto-selfport.jpg

name: Frans Hals
bio: A Haarlem portraitist whose loose, lively brushwork captured fleeting expressions. Impressionists such as Manet admired him greatly.
bio_full: Frans Hals was born in Antwerp, but his Protestant family moved north to Haarlem after Antwerp fell to Spanish forces in 1585. He spent his whole career there. He was the city's leading portraitist, painting merchants, preachers and their wives, as well as large group portraits of Haarlem's civic militia companies and the governors of charitable institutions. He also painted lively genre heads of drinkers, musicians and laughing children. Despite his success he often had money troubles, and in old age he received a small pension from the city. He died in Haarlem in 1666, and the museum there bears his name.

Hals is famous for his loose, rapid, visible brushwork, which seems to catch his sitters' expressions mid-word or mid-laugh. His portraits feel spontaneous and full of life compared with the polished finish of his contemporaries. After falling out of fashion he was enthusiastically rediscovered in the 19th century, when Manet, Courbet, Van Gogh and the American painter John Singer Sargent admired the freedom of his handling.
portrait_file: After Frans Hals - Portrait of Frans Hals - Indianapolis.jpg
portrait_caption: Portrait of Frans Hals, copy after a lost original, Indianapolis Museum of Art

name: Nicolas Poussin
bio: The founder of French classical painting, who worked mostly in Rome on ordered, intellectual scenes from mythology, history and the Bible.
bio_full: Nicolas Poussin was born in Normandy and trained in Paris. In 1624 he went to Rome, where he spent almost all the rest of his life. There he found learned patrons such as the antiquarian Cassiano dal Pozzo and painted for a circle of connoisseurs who appreciated his serious, intellectual approach. Louis XIII and Cardinal Richelieu summoned him back to Paris in 1640 as First Painter to the King, but he disliked court intrigue and the large decorative commissions, and returned to Rome in 1642.

Poussin painted mythological, historical and biblical subjects with carefully planned compositions, clear drawing, measured gesture and a stoic moral seriousness inspired by antiquity and Raphael. He believed a painting should be read like a text, with each figure's expression conveying meaning. His late landscapes are among the most profound in art. Through the French Royal Academy, where the 'Poussinistes' (championing drawing) famously argued against the 'Rubénistes' (championing colour), he became the founding father of French classicism and a model for David and Cézanne.
portrait_file: Nicolas Poussin 078.jpg

name: Anthony van Dyck
bio: Rubens's most gifted assistant, who became principal painter to Charles I of England. His elegant aristocratic portraits set the model for British portraiture.
bio_full: Anthony van Dyck was a prodigy in Antwerp, running his own workshop as a teenager and becoming Rubens's most gifted assistant. From 1621 to 1627 he worked in Italy, above all in Genoa, where he painted elegant full-length portraits of the city's aristocracy and studied Titian closely. After a few years back in Antwerp he moved to London in 1632 as principal painter to Charles I, who knighted him. He painted the king, Queen Henrietta Maria, their children and the English nobility until his early death in London in 1641.

Van Dyck created a new kind of aristocratic portrait: relaxed yet dignified, elegant, refined, with shimmering silks, slender hands and poetic landscape backgrounds. His images of Charles I shaped the king's legend, and his style became the standard for British portraiture for two centuries, through Lely, Kneller, Gainsborough and Reynolds. He also left a famous series of etched portraits of his fellow artists, the Iconography.
portrait_file: Anthony van Dyck - Self-portrait with a Sunflower.jpg

name: William Hogarth
bio: Painter, printmaker and satirist who invented the 'modern moral subject', narrative series sold as popular engravings.
bio_full: William Hogarth was born in London and trained as an engraver of silver before taking up painting. He eloped with the daughter of the court painter Sir James Thornhill. His first great success, the series A Harlot's Progress (1732), was sold to the public as engravings, and its popularity led to pirated copies. Hogarth campaigned for the Engraving Copyright Act of 1735, known as 'Hogarth's Act', which protected artists' rights in their prints. He was a founding governor of the Foundling Hospital, created famous prints such as Gin Lane and Beer Street (1751), and wrote a treatise, The Analysis of Beauty (1753), arguing for the S-shaped 'line of beauty'.

Hogarth called his narrative series 'modern moral subjects'. They are stories told in sequences of pictures, read like a novel or play, satirising greed, vanity, corruption, cruelty and fashionable folly in every class of London society. He was also a lively portraitist and a fierce promoter of a native British school of painting against fashionable foreign imports. His work is a forerunner of the political cartoon and the comic strip.
portrait_file: The Painter and His Pug by William Hogarth.jpg

name: Canaletto
bio: The master of the Venetian veduta (city view), hugely popular with British Grand Tour travellers.
bio_full: Giovanni Antonio Canal, called Canaletto ('little canal'), was the son of a Venetian theatrical scene painter and began his career painting stage sets. Around 1720 he turned to painting views of Venice. These became the most coveted souvenirs of British travellers on the Grand Tour, many sold through his agent Joseph Smith, the British consul, whose own huge collection was later bought by George III for the Royal Collection. When the War of the Austrian Succession cut off the tourist trade, he moved to England in 1746 and spent most of the next decade painting London and country houses.

Canaletto's vedute (view paintings) combine topographical accuracy with careful composition, crisp light and lively figures. He often adjusted viewpoints and combined several perspectives into one picture. He owned a camera obscura, now in the Museo Correr in Venice, and used drawing aids to construct his views. His early work is loose and atmospheric. His later, more mechanical production was supported by a busy workshop and many imitators, including his nephew Bernardo Bellotto.

name: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo
bio: The greatest decorative painter of the 18th century, filling palace ceilings across Europe with luminous skies and figures.
bio_full: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was born in Venice and married Cecilia Guardi, sister of the view painters Francesco and Gianantonio Guardi. He became the most sought-after decorative painter in Europe, covering ceilings and walls with frescoes in Venetian palaces and churches, in the Villa Pisani at Stra and in northern Italy. In 1750–53 he worked in Würzburg for the Prince-Bishop. In 1762 King Charles III summoned him to Madrid to paint ceilings in the new Royal Palace, and he died there in 1770. His sons Giandomenico and Lorenzo were his assistants.

Tiepolo's frescoes open ceilings into dazzling skies filled with gods, allegories and exotic figures, foreshortened from below, in luminous pastel colour and with tremendous speed and confidence. He also made witty etchings and brilliant oil sketches. By the end of his life, Neoclassical taste was turning against his flamboyant style, but he is now seen as the last great master of the Italian grand decorative tradition.
portrait_file: Tiepolo, Giovanni Battista - Fresken Treppenhaus des Würzburger Residenzschlosses, Szenen zur Apotheose des Fürstbischofs, Detail Giovanni Battista Tiepolo - 1750-1753.jpg
portrait_caption: Self-portrait in the staircase fresco of the Würzburg Residence, 1752–53

name: Jean-Siméon Chardin
bio: A painter of still lifes and quiet domestic scenes, admired for his textured paint and truth to everyday life.
bio_full: Jean-Siméon Chardin, the son of a Parisian maker of billiard tables, spent his whole life in Paris and almost never left it. In 1728 the Royal Academy admitted him as a painter 'of animals and fruit', the lowest category in its hierarchy of genres, on the strength of The Ray and The Buffet. From the 1730s he also painted quiet scenes of servants and middle-class family life, such as Saying Grace and Soap Bubbles. He later served as the Academy's treasurer and arranged the paintings at its Salon exhibitions. When failing eyesight made oil painting hard, he turned to pastel, producing memorable late self-portraits in spectacles.

Chardin's still lifes of copper pots, bread, fruit and game are painted with a thick, granular, almost tactile paint and soft harmonies of colour that give humble objects great dignity. The philosopher Diderot praised his work as magic in his Salon reviews. Chardin was admired as a counterweight to the frivolity of the Rococo, and he later inspired Cézanne, Morandi and many still-life painters.
portrait_file: Chardin pastel selfportrait.jpg

name: François Boucher
bio: The favourite painter of Madame de Pompadour and first painter to Louis XV, the embodiment of Rococo decoration and pastoral fantasy.
bio_full: François Boucher was born in Paris and trained with François Lemoyne. He made his name engraving Watteau's drawings and won the Prix de Rome, studying in Italy from 1727 to 1731. Back in Paris he rose rapidly at court. He designed tapestries for the Beauvais and Gobelins manufactories, becoming director of the Gobelins in 1755, as well as stage sets, porcelain and book illustrations. In 1765 he became First Painter to King Louis XV. His most important patron was Madame de Pompadour, the king's mistress, whose portraits he painted several times and whom he reportedly taught to etch.

Boucher embodied the Rococo: pastel-coloured mythologies of Venus and her nymphs, pastoral scenes of shepherds and shepherdesses, and frankly erotic nudes, painted with brilliant decorative fluency. His prodigious output decorated palaces across Europe. Critics like Diderot attacked him as artificial and immoral, and his reputation fell with the rise of Neoclassicism. His pupil Fragonard carried his style into the next generation.
portrait_file: Boucher par Gustav Lundberg 1741.jpg

name: Thomas Gainsborough
bio: A leading British portrait and landscape painter and founder member of the Royal Academy, with a light, feathery touch.
bio_full: Thomas Gainsborough was born in Sudbury, Suffolk. He went to London at about 13 and trained with the French engraver Hubert Gravelot. He returned to Suffolk, painting portraits and landscapes in Sudbury and Ipswich, then moved in 1759 to the fashionable spa town of Bath, where he became a successful society portraitist. In 1768 he was a founder member of the Royal Academy. He settled in London in 1774, where he was patronised by George III and Queen Charlotte, competing with Sir Joshua Reynolds as the leading portraitist of the age.

Gainsborough said he painted portraits for money and landscapes for love. His portraits are elegant and informal, painted with light, feathery strokes and silvery colour, and often set in landscape settings inspired by Van Dyck. His landscapes and 'fancy pictures' of rustic children helped found the English landscape tradition that led to Constable.
portrait_file: Thomas Gainsborough by Thomas Gainsborough.jpg

name: Henry Fuseli
bio: A Swiss-born painter in London who specialised in the supernatural, dreams and dramatic literary scenes.
bio_full: Johann Heinrich Füssli was born in Zürich, the son of a painter and writer, and was ordained as a Zwinglian minister. In 1762 he had to leave Switzerland after helping to expose a corrupt magistrate. He settled in London, where Sir Joshua Reynolds encouraged him to become a painter. He spent 1770–78 in Rome studying Michelangelo, then returned to London, anglicised his name to Henry Fuseli and became one of the most original artists of the Royal Academy, eventually its Professor of Painting and Keeper. He was a friend of William Blake and of the philosopher Mary Wollstonecraft.

Fuseli painted dramatic, sometimes violent and erotic scenes from Shakespeare, Milton, Dante and Germanic legend, as well as dreams and the supernatural. His figures are muscular, contorted and theatrically lit. He projected a Milton Gallery and contributed to John Boydell's Shakespeare Gallery. His fascination with the irrational and the subconscious makes him a forerunner of Romanticism and Symbolism.
portrait_file: Henry Fuseli by James Northcote.jpg

name: William Blake
bio: Poet, painter and printmaker who invented relief etching to combine his own text and images into visionary illuminated books.
bio_full: William Blake was born in London, the son of a hosier, and was apprenticed to the engraver James Basire, for whom he drew the tombs of Westminster Abbey. He studied briefly at the Royal Academy Schools, married Catherine Boucher (whom he taught to read and who helped him print and colour his books), and earned a modest living as an engraver. In 1788 he developed 'relief etching', which he said had been revealed to him in a vision by his dead brother Robert. With it he printed text and image together in illuminated books such as Songs of Innocence and of Experience (1789–94) and his prophetic books. In 1804 he was tried for sedition after a dispute with a soldier and acquitted. He died in London in 1827.

Blake created a private mythology of figures such as Urizen, Los and Orc to explore reason, imagination, tyranny, religion and revolution. He worked in watercolour, tempera, engraving and colour printing, with sinuous lines and muscular figures influenced by Michelangelo and medieval art. He was little known and often thought mad in his lifetime. The Pre-Raphaelites rediscovered him, and he is now celebrated as one of England's greatest poets and visionary artists. His lyric 'And did those feet in ancient time' became the hymn Jerusalem.
portrait_file: William Blake by Thomas Phillips.jpg

name: Rosa Bonheur
bio: The most famous woman painter of the 19th century, celebrated for animal paintings based on close study. She was the first woman artist awarded the Legion of Honour.
bio_full: Rosa Bonheur was born in Bordeaux, the daughter of the painter and drawing teacher Raymond Bonheur, a follower of the utopian Saint-Simonian movement. He encouraged her to train as an artist. To study animal anatomy she visited slaughterhouses, horse fairs and veterinary schools, and she obtained a police permit allowing her to wear trousers for this work. She won a gold medal at the Salon in 1848, and Ploughing in the Nivernais (1849) and The Horse Fair made her internationally famous, especially in Britain and the United States. In 1865 Empress Eugénie presented her with the Legion of Honour, the first time it was given to a woman artist.

Bonheur lived for decades with her partner Nathalie Micas, and later with the American painter Anna Klumpke, at the Château de By near Fontainebleau, where she kept a menagerie including lions, deer and horses. Her animal paintings combine scientific accuracy with energy and grandeur. She was the most successful woman artist of the 19th century and has become an icon of independence and of lesbian history.

name: John Everett Millais
bio: A child prodigy and co-founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood who later became President of the Royal Academy.
bio_full: John Everett Millais was a child prodigy: at 11 he became the youngest student ever admitted to the Royal Academy Schools. In 1848, with William Holman Hunt and Dante Gabriel Rossetti, he founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. His Christ in the House of His Parents (1850) was attacked by Charles Dickens for its unidealised realism, but the critic John Ruskin defended the group. In 1855 he married Effie Gray, whose marriage to Ruskin had been annulled. In later life he became a hugely successful painter of portraits, landscapes and sentimental subjects. His painting Bubbles was famously used to advertise Pears soap. He was made a baronet and in 1896 became President of the Royal Academy, shortly before his death.

Millais's early Pre-Raphaelite work is distinguished by brilliant, jewel-like colour on a white ground, minute botanical accuracy painted outdoors from nature, and intense emotional storytelling. His later broader, looser style made him one of the richest artists of the Victorian age.
portrait_file: Sir John Everett Millais, 1st Bt by Charles Robert Leslie.jpg

name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
bio: Poet and painter, co-founder of the Pre-Raphaelites, whose later images of brooding women shaped Aestheticism and Symbolism.
bio_full: Dante Gabriel Rossetti was born in London, the son of Gabriele Rossetti, an Italian political exile and Dante scholar. His sister was the poet Christina Rossetti. In 1848 he co-founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood with Millais and Hunt. He was as much a poet as a painter and also made translations from early Italian poetry. In 1860 he married his model Elizabeth Siddal, who died of a laudanum overdose in 1862. Grief-stricken, he buried a manuscript of his poems with her, and later had it recovered from her grave. From the 1860s his principal muse was Jane Morris, wife of his friend William Morris, with whom he shared Kelmscott Manor. He became dependent on chloral and died in 1882.

Rossetti's early works are medieval scenes in bright, flat colour. From the 1860s he painted mostly sensuous half-length images of women with abundant hair, full lips and strong necks, surrounded by flowers and symbolic objects, often paired with his own sonnets. These became the defining images of Aestheticism and influenced the Symbolists and Art Nouveau.
portrait_file: William Holman Hunt - Portrait of Dante Gabriel Rossetti at 22 years of Age - Google Art Project.jpg

name: James McNeill Whistler
bio: An American based in London and Paris who championed 'art for art's sake', titling his paintings like musical compositions.
bio_full: James Abbott McNeill Whistler was born in Lowell, Massachusetts, and spent part of his childhood in St Petersburg, where his father worked as a railway engineer for the tsar. He was dismissed from the West Point military academy, worked briefly as a map engraver, and in 1855 went to Paris to study art, never returning to America. He settled in London in 1859. His Symphony in White, No. 1 was a sensation at the Paris Salon des Refusés in 1863. In 1877 the critic John Ruskin accused him of 'flinging a pot of paint in the public's face' with a painted Nocturne. Whistler sued for libel and won, but the damages were a single farthing, and the legal costs bankrupted him in 1879.

Whistler believed in 'art for art's sake': a painting should be an arrangement of colours and forms, like music, rather than a story or moral lesson. So he titled works Symphonies, Harmonies, Arrangements and Nocturnes. He was influenced by Japanese prints, was a superb etcher (above all of Venice), designed the Peacock Room (now in the Freer Gallery, Washington), and was a witty, combative public figure who signed with a butterfly monogram.
portrait_file: Whistler Selbstporträt.jpg

name: John Singer Sargent
bio: The leading society portraitist of his era, known for dazzling, fluent brushwork.
bio_full: John Singer Sargent was born in Florence to American expatriate parents and grew up travelling around Europe. He trained in Paris from 1874 with the portraitist Carolus-Duran and made his name at the Salon with portraits and the Spanish dance scene El Jaleo. The scandal over Madame X in 1884 prompted him to move to London, where he painted Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose (Tate) and became the most fashionable portraitist on both sides of the Atlantic. Around 1907 he largely gave up formal portraiture in favour of landscapes, watercolours and murals for the Boston Public Library and Museum of Fine Arts. As an official war artist in the First World War, he painted the monumental Gassed (Imperial War Museum).

Sargent's brushwork is fluent, bold and economical, influenced by Velázquez and Hals. He captured the glamour and nervous elegance of the Edwardian elite, as well as sparkling light in his watercolours of Venice, the Alps and the Middle East. He produced around 900 oil paintings and more than 2,000 watercolours.

name: Camille Pissarro
birthplace: Charlotte Amalie, St Thomas (Danish West Indies)
bio: The only artist to exhibit in all eight Impressionist exhibitions and a generous mentor to Cézanne and Gauguin.
bio_full: Camille Pissarro was born on the Caribbean island of St Thomas, then a Danish colony, to a Sephardic Jewish family of French and Portuguese origin. After working in the family store he moved to Paris in 1855, where he was influenced by Corot. During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 he took refuge in London, studied Constable and Turner, and met the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel. The Prussian army occupied his house in Louveciennes and destroyed many of his paintings. Back in France he lived in Pontoise, where he painted side by side with Cézanne, and later in Éragny. He was the only artist to show at all eight Impressionist exhibitions.

Pissarro was the patriarch and teacher of Impressionism: generous, open-minded and politically committed to anarchism. He mentored Cézanne, Gauguin and others. He painted rural landscapes, markets and peasants, and from 1885 to 1890 he experimented with the dot technique of Seurat's Neo-Impressionism. In his last years an eye infection forced him to work indoors, and he painted series of Paris, Rouen and Le Havre from hotel windows. His sons, including Lucien, also became painters.

name: Mary Cassatt
bio: An American in Paris invited by Degas to join the Impressionists, best known for intimate scenes of women and children.
bio_full: Mary Cassatt was born near Pittsburgh into a wealthy family, studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and moved to Europe in 1866, eventually settling in Paris. After several Salon successes, Degas invited her in 1877 to exhibit with the Impressionists, and she showed with them four times. She was profoundly influenced by an 1890 exhibition of Japanese prints and produced a celebrated series of colour prints combining drypoint and aquatint. In 1893 she painted a large mural, Modern Woman, for the Woman's Building at the Chicago World's Fair, which is now lost. She advised American collectors, especially Louisine and Henry Havemeyer, whose collection went to the Metropolitan Museum. Her eyesight failed from about 1914, and she died in France in 1926.

Cassatt is best known for intimate scenes of women's daily lives: reading, taking tea, dressing, and above all caring for children. She depicted the bond between mother and child without sentimentality. She was a supporter of women's suffrage and the most important American member of the Impressionist movement.

name: Gustave Caillebotte
bio: A painter and wealthy patron of the Impressionists, known for steep perspectives of Haussmann's new Paris. He bequeathed his collection to the French state.
bio_full: Gustave Caillebotte was born in Paris to a very wealthy family, earned a law degree and served in the Franco-Prussian War before studying painting with Léon Bonnat. After the Salon rejected The Floor Scrapers in 1875, he joined the Impressionists, exhibiting from 1876, and became a key organiser and financial backer of their shows. He also bought many of their paintings, sometimes to support struggling friends. He was a passionate yachtsman and boat designer, a stamp collector with his brother Martial and a keen gardener at Petit-Gennevilliers. He died there in 1894, aged 45. He left his collection of Impressionist works to the French state, which after much controversy accepted part of it. It became the core of the Musée d'Orsay's Impressionist collection.

Caillebotte's own painting combines Impressionist light with a more precise, realist approach. He was fascinated by the new Paris of Baron Haussmann's boulevards, steep plunging perspectives, views from balconies and windows, and urban labourers and bourgeois men. Long seen mainly as a patron, he has been reassessed since the 1970s as a major painter.

name: Henri Rousseau
bio: A self-taught customs official ('Le Douanier') whose flat, dreamlike jungles were mocked at first and then embraced by the avant-garde.
bio_full: Henri Rousseau was born in Laval in western France, the son of a tinsmith. After army service he worked for many years as a toll collector at the gates of Paris, which earned him the nickname 'Le Douanier' (the customs officer). He was entirely self-taught and began exhibiting at the Salon des Indépendants in 1886, where critics and the public mocked his work for decades. He retired in 1893 to paint full time, supporting himself by teaching and playing music. He never left France, and his famous jungles were drawn from visits to the Paris botanical gardens and zoo, illustrated magazines and his imagination. He died in Paris in 1910.

Rousseau's flat, meticulously detailed, dreamlike pictures, with lush vegetation, staring animals and naive perspective, were championed by avant-garde artists and poets. In 1908 Picasso and friends held a famous banquet in his honour at the Bateau-Lavoir studio, half in jest and half in homage. He became a hero of modernism and the best-known 'naive' painter, and he influenced the Surrealists.

name: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
bio: The chronicler of Montmartre's cabarets, dance halls and brothels, whose bold posters transformed graphic design.
bio_full: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was born in Albi into an ancient aristocratic family. His parents were first cousins, and he probably had a congenital bone disorder. After breaking both thigh bones in his early teens, his legs stopped growing, and he reached an adult height of about 1.5 metres. He studied painting in Paris with Léon Bonnat and Fernand Cormon, where he met Van Gogh and Émile Bernard, and he settled in Montmartre. His poster Moulin Rouge – La Goulue (1891) made him famous overnight. He spent his nights in cabarets, dance halls, circuses and brothels. Alcoholism ruined his health, and after a stay in a sanatorium in 1899 he died in 1901, aged 36, at his mother's château.

Toulouse-Lautrec captured the performers and customers of Montmartre's nightlife, including Jane Avril, Aristide Bruant, Yvette Guilbert and La Goulue, with sharp, economical line, bold colour and a sympathetic but unflinching eye. His lithographic posters, influenced by Japanese prints and Degas, revolutionised graphic design and advertising. The Musée Toulouse-Lautrec in Albi holds the world's largest collection of his work.

name: Egon Schiele
bio: A protégé of Klimt whose angular, raw self-portraits and nudes are central to Austrian Expressionism. He died at 28 in the 1918 flu pandemic.
bio_full: Egon Schiele was born in Tulln on the Danube, where his father was stationmaster. His father died when Egon was 14. He entered the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts at 16 but left after three years, rebelling against its conservatism. Gustav Klimt became his mentor and supporter. With his companion and model Wally Neuzil he moved to the small town of Neulengbach, where in 1912 he was arrested and briefly imprisoned. Most charges were dropped, but he was convicted for exhibiting erotic drawings where children could see them. In 1915 he married Edith Harms and was called up for military service. His exhibition at the Vienna Secession in 1918 was a great success, but that autumn Edith, six months pregnant, died of influenza, and Schiele died three days later, aged 28.

Schiele's art is defined by its nervous, angular line and its raw, often contorted and sexual images of the human body, including dozens of unsparing self-portraits. He also painted townscapes and landscapes. He is a central figure of Austrian Expressionism, and the Leopold Museum in Vienna has the world's largest collection of his work.

name: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner
bio: A founder of Die Brücke in Dresden, whose jagged forms and clashing colours express the tension of the modern city.
bio_full: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner was born in Aschaffenburg in Bavaria and studied architecture in Dresden. In 1905, with fellow architecture students Erich Heckel, Karl Schmidt-Rottluff and Fritz Bleyl, he founded the artists' group Die Brücke ('The Bridge'), aiming to build a bridge to the future. They painted nudes in the studio and outdoors at the Moritzburg lakes, and they revived woodcut as a raw, expressive medium. In 1911 he moved to Berlin, where he painted his famous street scenes of prostitutes and passers-by. Drafted in the First World War, he suffered a breakdown and moved to Switzerland in 1917, settling near Davos, where he painted the mountains and their farmers. In 1937 the Nazis declared him 'degenerate' and removed over 600 of his works from German museums. He took his own life in 1938.

Kirchner's art, with its jagged forms, flattened space, clashing non-naturalistic colours and influences from African and Oceanic art and German Gothic woodcuts, expresses the excitement, alienation and nervous tension of modern life. He is one of the leading figures of German Expressionism.

name: Franz Marc
bio: Co-founder of Der Blaue Reiter who painted animals in symbolic colours. He was killed in the First World War.
bio_full: Franz Marc was born in Munich, the son of a painter. After studying theology and then art at the Munich Academy, he visited Paris and was deeply affected by Van Gogh and the Impressionists. He studied animal anatomy in depth. His friendships with August Macke and Wassily Kandinsky led to the founding of the Blue Rider (Der Blaue Reiter) in 1911, and they published an influential almanac in 1912. Marc volunteered for the army in 1914 and was killed by a shell splinter at Verdun on 4 March 1916, aged 36.

Marc believed animals were purer and closer to nature and the spiritual than humans. He painted horses, deer, cows, tigers and foxes in symbolic colours: in his system blue stood for the masculine and spiritual, yellow for the feminine and gentle, and red for brutal matter. Under the influence of Cubism and Futurism his late works, such as The Fate of the Animals (1913), move towards abstraction.

name: Paul Klee
bio: A Bauhaus teacher whose witty, musical and childlike images explore colour, line and imagination.
bio_full: Paul Klee was born at Münchenbuchsee near Bern to a musical family and was himself an accomplished violinist. He studied art in Munich, associated with the Blue Rider group, and in 1914 travelled to Tunisia with August Macke and Louis Moilliet. There he had a revelation about colour, writing in his diary that colour and he were now one, and that he was a painter. He taught at the Bauhaus from 1921 to 1931 and then at the Düsseldorf Academy, until the Nazis dismissed him in 1933. He returned to Bern, and more than 100 of his works were seized from German museums as 'degenerate'. Despite a serious illness from 1935 he was extraordinarily productive in his last years. He died in 1940.

Klee produced around 10,000 works of great variety: drawings, watercolours, oils and puppets. He combined childlike simplicity, irony, music, poetry, writing and signs, colour theory and fantasy. His teaching notes are among the most important texts on modern art. The Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern holds the largest collection of his work.

name: Amedeo Modigliani
bio: A Paris-based painter and sculptor whose elongated faces and nudes draw on African and archaic sculpture. He died at 35.
bio_full: Amedeo Modigliani was born in Livorno, Italy, to a Sephardic Jewish family. Often ill with tuberculosis as a youth, he studied art in Florence and Venice and moved to Paris in 1906, living first in Montmartre and then in Montparnasse. Under the influence of Brâncuși and African and archaic sculpture, he devoted himself to carving stone heads between about 1909 and 1914, but the dust and cost forced him back to painting. He painted portraits of his friends, including Chaim Soutine, Juan Gris, Jean Cocteau and his dealer Léopold Zborowski, and of his companion Jeanne Hébuterne. His only solo exhibition in his lifetime, at the Berthe Weill gallery in 1917, was closed by the police on opening day because of its nudes. Weakened by poverty, alcohol and drugs, he died of tubercular meningitis in Paris in January 1920, aged 35.

Modigliani's style is instantly recognisable: elongated faces and necks, almond-shaped eyes often left blank, simplified, sculptural forms, warm colour and flowing outlines. His legend of bohemian poverty and early death has made him a symbol of the Paris art world, and his paintings are now among the most expensive in the world.

name: Umberto Boccioni
bio: The leading painter and sculptor of Futurism, who sought to represent movement and dynamism. He died after a fall from a horse during military training.
bio_full: Umberto Boccioni was born in Reggio Calabria and grew up in various parts of Italy. In Rome he studied with the Divisionist painter Giacomo Balla. In 1909 the poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti published the Futurist Manifesto in Le Figaro, praising speed, machines, violence and modernity. The next year Boccioni co-signed the Manifesto of Futurist Painters and became the movement's leading artist, with paintings such as The City Rises (1910) and the series States of Mind. In 1912 he wrote a technical manifesto of Futurist sculpture. A fervent supporter of Italy's entry into the First World War, he volunteered in 1915 and died in 1916 after falling from a horse during cavalry training near Verona, aged 33.

Boccioni tried to show movement, energy and the fusion of objects with their surroundings, which he called 'dynamism' and 'lines of force'. He drew on Cubist fragmentation and Divisionist colour. His sculpture, in particular, broke down the boundary between figure and space. The Futurists' glorification of war and the movement's later links with Fascism complicate their legacy.

name: Kazimir Malevich
bio: The founder of Suprematism, an abstraction of pure geometric form and 'the supremacy of pure feeling'.
bio_full: Kazimir Malevich was born in Kyiv to a Polish family and grew up in rural Ukraine before moving to Moscow in 1904. He passed rapidly through Impressionism, Symbolism and a Russian 'Cubo-Futurism'. In 1913 he designed the costumes and sets for the Futurist opera Victory over the Sun, including a curtain with a black and white square. At the exhibition 0,10 in Petrograd in December 1915 he unveiled Suprematism, an art of pure geometric forms, with the Black Square as its emblem. After the Revolution he taught in Vitebsk, where he founded the UNOVIS group, and later in Petrograd. Under Stalin's regime he was attacked as a formalist and briefly arrested in 1930. In his last years he returned to stylised figure painting. He died in Leningrad in 1935, and a black square was painted on his coffin.

Malevich sought the 'supremacy of pure feeling' in art, free from the depiction of objects. His White on White (1918) took this further than anyone at the time. He was a major influence on Constructivism, the Bauhaus and later Minimalism. In recent years there has been growing emphasis on his Ukrainian roots.

name: Constantin Brâncuși
bio: A pioneer of modern sculpture who reduced forms to their pure essence in polished bronze, marble and carved wood.
bio_full: Constantin Brâncuși was born into a peasant family in the village of Hobița in Romania. He worked as a shepherd and a shop boy as a child, studied at the school of arts and crafts in Craiova and the Bucharest School of Fine Arts, and then made his way to Paris in 1904, partly on foot. He worked briefly as an assistant in Rodin's studio in 1907 but left after a short time, reportedly saying that nothing grows in the shadow of great trees. He spent the rest of his life in Paris. His ensemble at Târgu Jiu in Romania, including the Endless Column (1938), is a memorial to Romanian soldiers of the First World War. He bequeathed his studio and its contents to the French state, and it has been reconstructed beside the Centre Pompidou.

Brâncuși carved directly in stone and wood and refined his forms in polished bronze. Rejecting the expressive modelling of Rodin, he pursued the simplified essence of his subjects in a few recurring themes: The Kiss, the Sleeping Muse, the head, the bird and the column. His pure, abstract forms and his treatment of bases as part of the sculpture make him one of the founders of modern sculpture and a forerunner of Minimalism.

name: Georgia O'Keeffe
bio: A key figure of American modernism, known for magnified flowers, New York skyscrapers and New Mexico landscapes.
bio_full: Georgia O'Keeffe was born on a farm near Sun Prairie, Wisconsin. She studied at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Art Students League in New York, and she worked as an art teacher in Texas and elsewhere. The ideas of Arthur Wesley Dow led her in 1915 to a series of radical charcoal abstractions, which the photographer and gallery owner Alfred Stieglitz exhibited in 1916. They married in 1924, and Stieglitz photographed her in hundreds of portraits. In the 1920s she painted her famous magnified flowers and New York skyscrapers. From 1929 she spent much of each year in New Mexico, moving there permanently after Stieglitz's death in 1946 and living at Ghost Ranch and Abiquiú. Macular degeneration largely ended her painting in the 1970s. She died in Santa Fe in 1986, aged 98.

O'Keeffe is one of the founding figures of American modernism. Her close-up flowers, bleached animal bones and desert landscapes are painted with smooth surfaces, bold colour and a strong sense of abstraction. She firmly rejected the Freudian interpretations critics imposed on her flowers. The Georgia O'Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe opened in 1997.

name: Grant Wood
bio: A leader of Regionalism who painted the rural Midwest in a crisp style inspired by Northern Renaissance painting.
bio_full: Grant Wood was born on a farm near Anamosa, Iowa, and grew up in Cedar Rapids after his father's death. He trained in crafts and design, taught art in the Cedar Rapids public schools, and made several trips to Europe in the 1920s. On a 1928 trip to Munich, to supervise the making of a stained-glass window, he was impressed by the clarity and detail of early Flemish and German painting. Back in Iowa, he developed his mature style and became, with Thomas Hart Benton and John Steuart Curry, one of the leaders of Regionalism, which celebrated rural Midwestern America. He founded an artists' colony at Stone City and taught at the University of Iowa. He died in 1942.

Wood's paintings, with their crisp outlines, smooth surfaces and stylised, rounded landscapes, depict the farms, people and legends of the Midwest. Whether his work is affectionate tribute, gentle satire or both remains a matter of debate. American Gothic made him famous overnight.

name: Willem de Kooning
bio: A leading gestural Abstract Expressionist whose violent, energetic brushwork never fully abandoned the figure.
bio_full: Willem de Kooning was born in Rotterdam and apprenticed at 12 to a firm of commercial artists and decorators while studying at night at the Rotterdam Academy. In 1926 he stowed away on a ship to the United States. He worked as a house painter and commercial artist and, during the Depression, for the Federal Art Project, and he formed a close friendship with Arshile Gorky. He married the painter Elaine Fried in 1943. His first solo exhibition, of black-and-white abstractions, was in 1948. The Woman series of the early 1950s caused a sensation. He moved permanently to Springs, East Hampton, in 1963. In his last years he developed Alzheimer's disease, and the late works he made in this period remain debated. He died in 1997.

De Kooning was a leading gestural Abstract Expressionist, but unlike Pollock he never fully abandoned the figure. His paintings are built from slashing, sweeping brushstrokes, layers of paint scraped and reworked, and a constant tension between abstraction and figuration, especially in his images of women and landscapes. One of his paintings, Interchange (1955), reportedly sold privately in 2015 for around $300 million.

name: Jean-Michel Basquiat
bio: Basquiat moved from street graffiti (as SAMO) to international fame, painting skulls, crowns, words and Black history. He died at 27.
bio_full: Jean-Michel Basquiat was born in Brooklyn to a Haitian father and a mother of Puerto Rican descent, who took him to museums as a child. At about seven he was hit by a car, and during his recovery his mother gave him a copy of the anatomy textbook Gray's Anatomy, which influenced his later imagery. As a teenager he left home and, with his friend Al Diaz, wrote enigmatic graffiti in Lower Manhattan under the tag SAMO. He showed at the Times Square Show in 1980 and the New York/New Wave exhibition in 1981, and by 1982 he was showing internationally, including at Documenta 7, as one of the youngest artists ever invited. He collaborated with Andy Warhol in 1984–85. He died of a drug overdose in his studio in August 1988, aged 27.

In just under a decade Basquiat produced around 1,000 paintings and more than 1,000 drawings. They combine raw, energetic figuration, skulls, crowns, words, lists, diagrams and cross-outs. They draw on African American and Caribbean history, jazz, comics, anatomy and art history, and confront racism, power and identity. In 2017 one of his skull paintings of 1982 sold at auction for $110.5 million, then a record for an American artist.
